whyWeCreated.heading: Why we created BillGoose
paragraphs: There is no doubt that running a home has become harder than it should be. Bills sit with different suppliers, prices and contracts regularly change, useful information is spread across emails, apps and online accounts and even after comparing prices, people are often left to manage everything themselves without proper support.

We created BillGoose to bring more common sense to the whole process. Our mission is to turn scattered household information into useful, insightful, actionable support, helping people save money, save time and avoid the headache.

hero.heading: Are Broadband, TV and Mobile Bundles Really Cheaper?

image.alt: Broadband, TV and mobile bundle comparison

blocks.text: Are broadband, TV and mobile bundles really cheaper?

blocks.heading: THE SHORT ANSWER
blocks.text: A bundle can be cheaper, but only if you would choose every part of it anyway. Ignore the headline discount for a moment. Compare the full cost of the bundle with the full cost of suitable separate deals, then check what happens to each service if you switch, move home or cancel early.

blocks.heading: Why bundles are tempting
paragraphs: There is a lot to like about putting broadband, TV and mobile with one provider: fewer accounts, one bill and less admin. Providers may also offer lower broadband prices, discounted household SIMs, inclusive streaming or sport and one-off rewards.
That convenience has a price when the package includes services you barely use or ties several contracts together. The only reliable test is to compare like with like over the whole minimum term.

blocks.heading: First, understand what is actually bundled
paragraphs: "Bundle" can mean one contract covering several services or separate contracts linked by customer discounts. Ask which arrangement applies. Contract lengths, renewal dates and cancellation rules may differ even when everything appears on one bill.

The best way to judge it: treat the offer as three separate decisions. Is the broadband right for your home? Is the TV worth paying for? Is the mobile plan competitive for the coverage and data you need? The bundle only wins if all three answers are yes.

blocks.heading: A simple way to do the maths

items.title: Start with what you need
items.description: Choose the broadband speed, TV content and mobile allowance that fit your household before looking at promotions.

items.title: Price separate deals
items.description: Find realistic stand-alone options that meet the same needs. A cut-price basic service is not a fair comparison.

items.title: Add every bundle cost
items.description: Include monthly payments, setup, activation, delivery, equipment and installation. Count cashback only if you will claim it.

items.title: Use the full minimum term
items.description: Compare both totals across the same 18-month or 24-month period, including any stated price changes.

items.title: Strip out unwanted extras
items.description: Do not assign value to channels, data or subscriptions you would not otherwise buy and use.

items.title: Check how you get out
items.description: Review end dates, early termination charges, home-move terms and the effect of cancelling one service.

blocks.heading: Where bundles tend to work well
items: You already pay for the included TV, sport or streaming services.
The broadband speed and mobile data allowance suit your real usage.
A household mobile discount applies to SIMs you genuinely need.
The full contract cost beats equivalent separate deals after fees and price changes.
The contract length fits your plans and you are unlikely to move home soon.

blocks.heading: Where they tend to go wrong
items: The package is built around a large TV pack you will hardly watch.
The mobile plan includes far more data than you use or has weaker coverage for you.
Introductory discounts end while the minimum term continues.
The services have different end dates or cannot be changed independently.
Leaving one part triggers charges or removes discounts from the rest.

blocks.heading: Check Each Service On Its Own Merits
paragraphs: Broadband: buy enough speed, not the biggest number. Think about how many people are online together and whether your household regularly streams in 4K, games, works from home or uploads large files. If the problem is poor Wi-Fi in one room, paying for a faster line may not solve it; better router placement or a mesh system may matter more.

TV: price the programmes you actually watch. List the paid channels, sport and streaming services used every month. Compare that list with the bundle and with buying the same content separately. Check whether subscriptions are included for the full term or only as a short promotion.

Mobile: coverage comes before the discount. A cheap SIM is poor value if the network is unreliable where you live, work and travel. Check coverage, data, roaming, contract length and any handset finance separately. To keep your number when changing network, text PAC to 65075. To switch and take a new number, text STAC to 75075.

blocks.heading: One Bundle Does Not Always Mean One Switching Process
paragraphs: One Touch Switch covers switches between UK residential fixed broadband providers: the new provider normally manages the move. Mobile, pay TV, streaming subscriptions and other add-ons may follow different processes. Confirm what will cancel automatically and what you must cancel yourself.
Switching the broadband element will not necessarily close every linked service. Get the cancellation position in writing before the switch completes.

items: The full contract cost is difficult to find or calculate.
The contract summary does not match the advertised offer.
Several extras have been included without a clear explanation of their value.
You cannot see exactly when and by how much the price will change.
Broadband, TV and mobile have different minimum terms or end dates.
A reward depends on a claim process or deadline that is easy to miss.
The provider cannot explain what happens if you move home.
The deal only looks attractive because of a handset or TV package you did not plan to buy.

blocks.heading: If Affordability Is The Main Concern
paragraphs: Check social tariffs before committing to a commercial bundle. These are lower-cost broadband and phone packages offered by some providers to people receiving certain benefits. Eligibility, speeds and prices vary by provider. They may not include premium TV or large mobile allowances, but the lower price and more flexible terms can make them a better fit.

blocks.heading: The Decision In One Minute
paragraphs: BUNDLE IT: Choose the bundle when every service suits you, the full-term cost is lower and you understand how to leave or change each part.
KEEP IT SEPARATE: Choose stand-alone deals when they are cheaper, give you better coverage or content or let you switch each service at the right time.

blocks.text: Start with the services your household actually needs, then compare price, speed, content, coverage and contract length. BillGoose helps you compare suitable broadband and TV deals; use the same full-cost test before adding mobile or any other extra.

hero.heading: When Is the Best Time to Switch Energy Supplier?

image.alt: Best time to switch energy supplier

blocks.text: When is the best time to switch energy supplier?

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: The best time to compare energy deals is whenever your current tariff is ending, your rates are changing, your household circumstances have changed or a clearly better deal could outweigh any exit fee. If you are on a fixed tariff, the final 49 days are especially important because you can normally switch without paying an exit fee. If you are on a standard variable tariff, you can usually switch at any time.

blocks.heading: There is no single best month for everyone
paragraphs: People often ask whether summer, winter or the weeks before an Ofgem price-cap change are the best time to switch. In practice, the right moment depends more on your tariff, your usage and the deals available than on the season.

Energy prices can move in either direction, and nobody can know with certainty whether today's fixed deal will beat future variable rates. Waiting for the perfect moment can mean spending months on an unsuitable tariff. A better approach is to identify the points when a comparison is particularly worthwhile, then judge the options using your own annual consumption and the full tariff terms.
The following situations are the strongest prompts to review your energy deal.

blocks.heading: Strongest prompts to review your energy deal

items.title: Your fixed tariff has 49 days or less remaining
items.description: Citizens Advice states that if a fixed tariff has 49 days or less left, you can switch without paying an exit fee. If 50 days or more remain, your supplier might charge an early-exit fee, so check the tariff terms. Add the tariff end date to your Billgoose account or calendar and begin comparing around seven weeks beforehand.

items.title: Your fixed deal is ending and the replacement tariff is unclear
items.description: Your supplier should tell you what happens when your fixed tariff ends. Do not assume the offered replacement is automatically competitive. Compare the estimated annual cost, unit rates, standing charges, contract length and exit fees with alternatives from other suppliers.

items.title: You are on a standard variable tariff
items.description: Customers on standard variable tariffs can generally switch at any time. These tariffs are covered by Ofgem's price cap, but the cap is not a guarantee that a default tariff is the cheapest option. It limits the unit rates and standing charges suppliers can charge, not the total amount you pay.

items.title: Your supplier announces a price or tariff change
items.description: A notification about changing rates, terms or payment arrangements is a good reason to review your position. Read the notice carefully: identify when the change takes effect, whether you can leave without a fee and what the new annual estimate would be for your usage.

items.title: Your energy use has changed
items.description: A tariff that suited you last year may no longer fit if your household has changed. Common triggers include moving home, working from home more often, installing an electric vehicle charger, adding solar panels, fitting a heat pump, changing from prepayment to direct debit or having more people living at the property.

items.title: A new deal could repay its exit fee
items.description: An exit fee does not always mean you should wait. If a substantially cheaper tariff is available, the saving over the remaining contract period might exceed the fee. Calculate the net benefit rather than looking at the fee alone.

blocks.heading: Net benefit of switching early

cells: Estimated saving over the remaining term
Exit fee for gas and/or electricity
Saving minus all leaving costs
Use the same annual-consumption assumptions
Check whether fees apply to each fuel
Switch only if the overall deal still makes sense

blocks.note: Remember that the future saving is an estimate, especially if you are comparing a fixed tariff with a variable tariff whose rates can change.

blocks.heading: Should you switch before winter?
paragraphs: Winter is when many households use the most gas and electricity, so entering the colder months on a competitive tariff can matter. However, autumn is not automatically the cheapest time to switch. Tariff prices reflect wholesale costs, supplier pricing and market conditions, not simply the outside temperature.

It is sensible to review your deal before higher winter usage begins, particularly if your fixed tariff is ending. But do not accept a poor deal just because winter is approaching, and do not wait until autumn if a suitable tariff is available earlier.

blocks.heading: Should you wait for the next price-cap announcement?
paragraphs: Ofgem updates the default-tariff price cap every three months. Announcements can provide useful context for customers on standard variable tariffs, but a price-cap forecast is not a promise and does not show what every fixed tariff will cost.

Waiting may be reasonable if your current tariff is competitive, has no imminent change and you want to see confirmed information. Switching sooner may be more appropriate if your tariff is ending, you are paying more than suitable alternatives or a fixed deal offers certainty you value. The decision should be based on your circumstances, not a single market prediction.

blocks.heading: Your switching timeline

items.title: 2 to 3 months before a fixed deal ends
items.description: Find your tariff end date, annual kWh use, payment method, meter type and current exit fee. Set a reminder for the 49-day window.

items.title: Within the final 49 days
items.description: Compare available tariffs. Check annual cost, unit rates, standing charges, contract term, meter compatibility and supplier service.

items.title: When you choose a deal
items.description: Confirm the tariff details and switching date. Domestic customers normally receive a 14-day cooling-off period.

items.title: During the switch
items.description: A switch requested as soon as possible should normally complete within five working days. Keep confirmation emails and provide meter readings when requested.

items.title: After the switch
items.description: Check the opening and final readings, review your final bill and make sure any credit balance is returned.

blocks.heading: Times when switching needs extra care
items: You owe money to your supplier. Debt can affect whether and how you switch, particularly for prepayment customers.
You pay your landlord rather than the supplier. The person responsible for the energy account usually controls the supplier choice.
Your home is on a heat network. Customers on heat networks cannot usually choose a different energy supplier in the same way.
You have Economy 7, another time-of-use tariff or a specialist meter. Confirm compatibility before switching.
Your supplier has failed. Follow Ofgem's advice and wait for a new supplier to be appointed rather than starting a new switch immediately.
You receive support linked to your supplier or tariff. Check whether switching affects any discount, vulnerability service or payment arrangement.

hero.heading: Broadband Contract Ending? Your Step-by-Step Switching Checklist

blocks.text: Broadband Contract Ending? Your Step-by-Step Switching Checklist

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: When your broadband contract is ending, check your end date, current price, out-of-contract price, speed, exit fees and any renewal offer. Compare new deals using the total contract cost, expected speed, setup fees, router quality and future price rises. Thanks to One Touch Switch, most broadband customers now only need to contact the new provider, who manages the switch.

blocks.heading: Why You Should Not Ignore The End Of Your Broadband Contract
paragraphs: Broadband contracts often start with an introductory price. When the minimum term ends, that price can change, and the deal that felt competitive when you signed up may no longer be the best option.

Your provider should send an end-of-contract notification before your minimum term ends and continue to provide best-tariff information at least annually if you stay out of contract. Treat that notification as a prompt to compare rather than a reason to automatically renew.

You do not always need to switch provider. Sometimes your current provider will offer a fair renewal. But comparing properly gives you evidence: you can switch, negotiate, move to a faster package, or choose a cheaper deal with confidence.

blocks.heading: Your step-by-step switching checklist

items.title: Find your contract end date
items.description: Check your bill, online account or end-of-contract notification. If you are still inside the minimum term, leaving early could trigger an exit fee.

items.title: Check what you pay now
items.description: Record the current monthly price, any discount, line rental, TV add-ons, router charges and expected price after the contract ends.

items.title: Check your real-world speed
items.description: Run speed tests near the router and in the rooms where you actually use broadband. Note whether the problem is the line speed or home Wi-Fi.

items.title: Decide what you need
items.description: Think about household size, streaming, gaming, working from home, video calls, smart devices and upload needs.

items.title: Compare total contract cost
items.description: Do not compare the monthly price alone. Include setup fees, delivery charges, future price rises, cashback, rewards and contract length.

items.title: Check speed guarantees
items.description: Look at estimated speed, minimum guaranteed speed and what happens if the provider cannot deliver the promised service.

items.title: Review switching details
items.description: Check installation date, router delivery, engineer visit, email address, landline number, TV services and any equipment you must return.

items.title: Keep records
items.description: Save order confirmation, contract summary, promised start date, old provider notice, engineer appointment and final bill.

blocks.heading: What happens under One Touch Switch?
paragraphs: One Touch Switch is designed to make broadband and landline switching easier. For most fixed-line broadband switches, you contact the provider you want to move to, give them the required details and they manage the switch with your old provider.

If your details match, your old provider sends important switching information, such as any charges and the services being affected. If you go ahead, the new provider arranges the switch date where possible. Once the new service is working, the old service should end automatically.

You might still need to handle some parts yourself if your package includes other services such as TV, or if you deliberately choose to manage your own switch with an overlap period. In those cases, make sure you understand what will and will not be cancelled automatically.

blocks.heading: Billgoose Tip
blocks.text: Before ordering, check exactly which services are switching. Broadband, landline and TV may not all move in the same way, especially if they are bundled together.

blocks.heading: Check exit fees before you move
paragraphs: If you are outside the minimum contract period, switching is usually much simpler. If you are still in contract, you may need to pay an early termination charge. This can make a cheaper-looking new deal less attractive.

Compare the saving against the fee. For example, a new deal that saves £8 a month over 12 months may not be worthwhile if leaving early costs significantly more than the saving. Some providers offer switching credits or buyout offers, but these can have conditions, claim deadlines and exclusions.

blocks.heading: Should you renew, haggle or switch?

cells: Useful if the renewal price is competitive and service has been reliable.
Useful if you like your provider but their renewal offer is weak.
Useful if another provider offers better price, speed, reliability or contract terms.
Check contract length, future price rises and whether the offer is available to new customers.
Use comparison results as evidence. Ask about loyalty deals, speed upgrades and removing unused extras.
Check installation date, equipment returns, number porting and any bundle implications.
Do not renew solely for convenience if the out-of-contract price is poor.
Get any offer in writing before agreeing.
Keep your old service active until the switch is confirmed.

blocks.heading: Watch out for mid-contract price rises
paragraphs: For new contracts, telecoms providers must now show any contractually agreed price rises upfront in pounds and pence, and explain when they happen. This makes it easier to compare deals, but it does not mean prices can never rise.

If a provider uses an unspecified price rise during the contract, Ofcom says customers must be given 30 days' notice and the right to exit penalty-free. Read the contract summary carefully before ordering.

blocks.heading: What if the switch goes wrong?
paragraphs: Most switches should be straightforward, but problems can still happen. Keep your order confirmation, promised start date, engineer appointment details and any messages from both providers.

Under Ofcom's automatic compensation scheme, eligible customers can receive compensation if a new broadband or landline service does not start on the agreed date, an engineer appointment is missed, or a loss of service is not fixed after two full working days. Compensation is normally paid automatically as a bill credit.

items: Do you use an email address from your current broadband provider? Check whether you can keep it and whether a charge applies.
Do you need to keep your landline number? Confirm number-porting details before ordering.
Do you have TV, sport, streaming or security services bundled with broadband? Check what happens to each service.
Do you rent your router or need to return equipment? Ask about return deadlines and non-return fees.
Are you eligible for a social tariff? If you receive certain benefits, a lower-cost broadband package may be available.
Will an engineer need access? Make sure the installation date works for your household.
Could mobile broadband or a full-fibre alternative be better at your address? Compare availability, not just brand names.

hero.heading: Credit Card APR Explained Without the Jargon

blocks.text: Credit Card APR Explained Without the Jargon

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: APR stands for Annual Percentage Rate. It is a yearly cost figure designed to help you compare credit products. On credit cards, APR is useful, but it is not the whole story. If you repay your full statement balance on time each month, you can usually avoid purchase interest. If you carry a balance, miss payments, withdraw cash or use transfers, the actual cost depends on the rate, fees, promotional period, repayment amount and how long the debt remains unpaid.

blocks.heading: What does APR actually mean?
paragraphs: APR is a way of showing the annual cost of borrowing. It includes the interest rate and certain compulsory charges, expressed as a yearly percentage. The idea is to give customers a benchmark so similar credit products can be compared more easily.

With credit cards, APR can be confusing because the card is flexible. You can spend, repay, carry a balance, transfer a balance, withdraw cash or pay in full. Each action can be treated differently, and different rates or fees may apply.

That is why APR should be treated as a starting point rather than the final answer. A card with a lower APR can still be poor value if it has high fees or if it does not match the way you plan to use it.

blocks.heading: Representative APR versus your personal APR
paragraphs: When a credit card advertises a representative APR, that does not guarantee that every successful applicant will receive that rate. MoneyHelper explains that representative APR only has to be offered to at least 51% of accepted customers, so others may be charged more.

Your personal APR is the rate the provider offers after assessing your application. It can depend on your credit history, income, existing debts, affordability, account behaviour and the provider's lending criteria.

blocks.heading: Plain English Version
blocks.text: Representative APR is the advertised example. Personal APR is the rate you may actually get. Guaranteed rate means the provider is telling you that rate will apply if you are accepted, but always check the wording.

blocks.heading: The different rates on a credit card

cells: Purchase APR
Normal spending on the card once any interest-free or promotional period ends.
This is the main rate for everyday purchases if you do not repay in full.
Balance transfer rate
Balances moved from another credit card.
A 0% period can help reduce interest, but a transfer fee may apply.
Money transfer rate
Money moved from the card to your bank account.
Can be useful in limited cases but often has fees and a later revert rate.
Cash advance rate
Cash withdrawals or cash-like transactions.
Interest is usually charged immediately and fees often apply.
Annual or monthly fee
A card membership charge.
A rewards card can look attractive until the fee is included.
Late-payment fee
Charged if you miss the required payment.
Can increase cost and may harm your credit record.
Foreign usage fee
Spending or cash withdrawal abroad.
Important if you plan to use the card overseas.

blocks.heading: If you pay in full, APR may not matter much
paragraphs: A credit card can be a convenient payment tool if you repay the full statement balance by the due date every month. In that situation, purchase interest is usually avoided because of the card's interest-free period on purchases.

That does not mean the card is free in every situation. Cash withdrawals, balance transfers, money transfers, foreign spending, annual fees and late payments can still create charges. The safest rule is to treat the full statement balance as the amount that needs clearing, not just the minimum payment.

blocks.heading: If you carry a balance, APR matters a lot
paragraphs: If you do not clear the full balance, interest can be added and the debt can take much longer to repay. The higher the APR and the lower the repayment, the more expensive the borrowing becomes.

Minimum repayments are designed to keep the account up to date, not to clear borrowing quickly. MoneyHelper gives an example where a £2,000 credit card balance at 22% APR with a 2.5% minimum payment could take 14 years to clear if only the minimum is paid.

blocks.heading: Avoid the Minimum-payment Trap
blocks.text: If you can afford to pay more than the minimum, doing so can reduce interest and shorten the repayment time. If you are struggling, speak to the provider and consider free debt advice rather than borrowing more.

blocks.heading: 0% does not always mean free
paragraphs: Many credit cards advertise 0% purchase periods, 0% balance transfer periods or 0% money transfer periods. These can be useful when used carefully, but the details matter.

blocks.heading: Check before you apply for a 0% card
items: Check when the 0% period ends and what the standard rate becomes afterwards.
Check whether a balance transfer or money transfer fee applies.
Make at least the required minimum payment on time every month.
Avoid new spending on a balance transfer card unless the purchase terms are also suitable.
Have a repayment plan before the promotional period ends.
Do not treat a 0% limit as extra income; it is still borrowed money.

blocks.heading: APR does not show every cost in the same way
paragraphs: APR helps compare similar borrowing, but credit card costs can depend heavily on behaviour. A rewards card with a high APR can be good value for someone who pays in full and uses the rewards well. The same card can be expensive for someone who carries a balance.

Cash withdrawals are a common example. Citizens Advice warns that when you take cash out on a credit card, interest is added straight away, even if you pay off the balance by the due date. There can also be a cash withdrawal fee.

Lower purchase APR
Annual fee and whether you carry a balance
Could be better for borrowing if the fee is low.
Card B
0% purchases for a set period
Revert rate and repayment plan
Useful for planned spending if cleared before interest starts.
Card C
Rewards or cashback
Annual fee and whether you pay in full
Good for disciplined spending, poor for carrying debt.
Card D
0% balance transfer
Transfer fee and length of 0% period
Useful for existing debt if repayments are affordable.

blocks.heading: How to compare credit cards properly

items.title: Start with how you will use the card
items.description: Everyday spending, a large purchase, existing debt, travel, rewards and emergency borrowing all point to different card types.

items.title: Use eligibility checkers first
items.description: MoneyHelper says eligibility calculators can show products you may qualify for without affecting your credit file.

items.title: Look beyond representative APR
items.description: Check whether the rate is guaranteed, representative or personalised after application.

items.title: Check every fee
items.description: Include annual fees, balance transfer fees, money transfer fees, cash fees, foreign usage charges and default charges.

items.title: Plan repayments before applying
items.description: Work out how much you can repay monthly and how quickly the balance would clear.

items.title: Read the summary box
items.description: Check purchase rate, promotional period, payment date, minimum repayment, cash withdrawal terms and default charges.

blocks.heading: When a higher APR might still be acceptable
paragraphs: A high APR is not automatically a problem if you never carry a balance and the card has benefits that are worth more than any fee. For example, some people choose reward, cashback or travel cards for perks while repaying in full every month.
But if there is any chance you will carry a balance, the APR becomes more important than rewards. Interest can quickly outweigh cashback, points or vouchers.

blocks.heading: When to be cautious
items: You are applying because you cannot afford regular bills or essentials.
You expect to make only minimum repayments for more than a short period.
You are using one credit card to pay another debt without a repayment plan.
You are close to your credit limit on existing cards.
You are tempted by rewards but may not clear the balance in full.
You are considering cash withdrawals on a credit card.
You are unsure whether the advertised APR is the rate you will actually get.
You have missed payments or are already under financial pressure.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare credit cards?
blocks.text: APR is important, but it should not be read in isolation. The right card depends on your purpose, eligibility, fees, promotional terms, repayment plan and how disciplined you are likely to be with borrowing.

hero.heading: Fixed vs Variable Energy Tariffs: Which Is Better for You?

blocks.text: Fixed vs Variable Energy Tariffs: Which Is Better for You?

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: A fixed tariff may suit you if you value more certainty about your unit rates and standing charges for an agreed period. A variable tariff may suit you if you prefer flexibility and are comfortable with prices moving up or down. Neither option guarantees the lowest total bill: your usage, tariff rates, standing charges, contract terms and future market changes all matter.

blocks.heading: What is the difference between fixed and variable tariffs?
paragraphs: The main difference is what can happen to the rates you are charged. On a fixed tariff, the unit rates and standing charges are normally set for the fixed term. On a variable tariff, those rates can change.

This does not mean a fixed tariff fixes your total bill. You still pay for the gas and electricity you use, so a cold winter, a larger household or increased appliance use can raise the amount you owe. The word 'fixed' relates to the tariff rates, not unlimited energy for one set price.

Most standard variable tariffs are protected by Ofgem's energy price cap in Great Britain. The cap limits the unit rates and standing charges suppliers can apply to eligible default tariffs, but it is not a cap on a household's total bill.

blocks.heading: Fixed and variable tariffs at a glance

cells: Rates
Normally remain the same for the agreed fixed term.
Can rise or fall in line with the tariff terms.
Total bill
Still changes with the amount of energy used.
Changes with both usage and any rate changes.
Contract
Usually has a defined term, often around 12 months but sometimes longer.
Usually continues without a fixed end date.
Exit fees
May apply if you leave early, subject to the tariff terms.
Standard variable tariffs do not usually have exit fees.
Price cap
Fixed tariffs are generally outside the default-tariff price cap.
Standard variable/default tariffs are generally covered by the cap.
Flexibility
Lower if an exit fee applies.
Usually easier to leave without a fee.

blocks.heading: How a fixed tariff works
paragraphs: When you choose a fixed tariff, the supplier agrees the unit rates and standing charges for a specified period. This can make budgeting easier because you know the rates will not change during that term, provided the supplier honours the contract.

Your monthly direct debit may still be adjusted. Suppliers often spread expected annual usage across monthly payments, and the payment can change if your actual usage or account balance is different from the estimate.

blocks.heading: Potential advantages of fixing
items: More certainty about the rates charged during the fixed period.
Protection from rate increases on standard variable tariffs during the term.
A clearer basis for household budgeting when combined with realistic usage estimates.
The possibility of securing a tariff that is cheaper than the current or future variable rate.

blocks.heading: Potential disadvantages of fixing
items: An exit fee may apply if you leave before the permitted switching window.
You might miss out if variable rates fall substantially.
A longer fix can tie you to rates that later become uncompetitive.
Special conditions may apply, such as payment method or smart meter requirements.

blocks.heading: How a variable tariff works
paragraphs: On a variable tariff, the supplier can change the unit rates and standing charges in line with the tariff terms. A standard variable tariff is often the default tariff a customer moves onto when a fixed deal ends.

Ofgem reviews the price cap every three months. For customers on capped standard variable tariffs, the applicable maximum rates can therefore change quarterly. Suppliers may charge below the cap, and regional and payment-method differences can affect the rates shown on a bill.

blocks.heading: Potential advantages of staying variable
items: Greater flexibility, usually without an exit fee.
You can benefit if capped or supplier rates fall.
There is no need to commit to a fixed term while your circumstances are uncertain.
It can be easier to switch later if a more suitable deal becomes available.

blocks.heading: Potential disadvantages of staying variable
items: Rates can rise, making future bills harder to predict.
You may remain on a default tariff without actively checking alternatives.
Price-cap headlines can be misleading if you treat the typical annual figure as your personal bill.
The lack of a contract end date can make it easy to postpone comparison.

blocks.heading: Important
blocks.text: The price cap is not a 'safe maximum bill'. It limits the rates used to calculate eligible standard variable tariffs. A household that uses more energy will pay more than the typical annual figure used in announcements.

blocks.heading: Which option is more likely to suit you?
columns: A fixed tariff may be worth considering if...
A variable tariff may be worth considering if...

cells: You value certainty about rates.
You want freedom to switch without an exit fee.
You expect to remain at the property for the contract period.
Your household circumstances may change soon.
The estimated annual cost is competitive.
You are comfortable with rates moving every few months.
You are comfortable with the exit fee and other conditions.
You want to wait for confirmed market information.
You would prefer protection from possible rate increases.
The current variable estimate compares well with available fixes.

blocks.heading: How to compare fixed and variable tariffs

items.title: Use the same consumption figures
items.description: Enter the same annual gas and electricity use for every tariff. Actual kWh figures usually give a more meaningful comparison than a broad household estimate.

items.title: Compare estimated annual cost
items.description: Do not compare only the monthly direct debit. Check the full-year estimate based on the same usage.

items.title: Review rates and standing charges
items.description: A low unit rate can be offset by a higher standing charge, especially for lower-use homes.

items.title: Include exit fees
items.description: If the fixed tariff has an exit fee, consider whether you are likely to move home or switch early.

items.title: Check the length of the fix
items.description: A short fix and a multi-year fix create different risks and levels of certainty.

items.title: Read the conditions
items.description: Check meter requirements, payment method, green claims, rewards and customer-service arrangements.

items.title: Consider uncertainty honestly
items.description: No one can guarantee where energy prices will move. Decide whether rate certainty or flexibility matters more to you.

blocks.heading: Should you fix because the price cap is going up?
paragraphs: A rising price cap is a reason to compare, not an automatic instruction to fix. A fixed tariff might protect you from the next variable-rate increase, but the fix could still be more expensive than remaining variable over the full term.

Compare the fixed tariff's estimated annual cost with the applicable variable tariff, then consider known cap changes, credible uncertainty and the length of the contract. Avoid relying on a single forecast.

blocks.heading: What about time-of-use tariffs?
paragraphs: Time-of-use tariffs charge different electricity rates at different times. They can benefit households able to move significant use to cheaper off-peak periods, such as electric vehicle charging or running appliances overnight. They can also cost more if most electricity is used at peak times.
These tariffs are a separate decision from a simple fixed-versus-variable choice. Check whether the off-peak savings fit your actual routine and whether a compatible smart meter is required.

blocks.heading: What happens when a fixed tariff ends?
paragraphs: If you do not choose another tariff, your supplier will normally move you onto its standard variable tariff. Your supplier should remind you before the contract ends.

Citizens Advice says that when a fixed tariff has 49 days or less remaining, you can switch without paying an exit fee. That window is a good time to compare your supplier's renewal offer with alternatives.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare fixed and variable deals?

hero.heading: Home Insurance Explained: Buildings, Contents and Combined Cover

blocks.text: Home Insurance Explained: Buildings, Contents and Combined Cover

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: Home insurance usually means buildings insurance, contents insurance or a combined buildings and contents policy. Buildings insurance protects the structure of the home and permanent fixtures. Contents insurance protects the things you would normally take with you if you moved. Homeowners often need both. Renters usually need contents cover only, because the landlord is normally responsible for buildings insurance. Combined cover can be simpler, but it is still important to compare the cover limits, exclusions, excesses and optional extras.

blocks.heading: What is home insurance?
paragraphs: Home insurance is designed to help put things right if your home or belongings are damaged, stolen or destroyed by an insured event. It is not one single product. Most policies are built around buildings cover, contents cover or both together.

The best policy is not always the cheapest. The important question is whether the policy would pay out enough, in the right circumstances, with an excess you could afford and exclusions you understand.
This guide explains the difference between buildings, contents and combined cover, then shows what to check before comparing quotes.

blocks.heading: Buildings, contents and combined cover at a glance

cells: Buildings
Structure of the home, permanent fixtures and fittings, such as walls, roof, floors, fitted kitchens and bathrooms.
Homeowners and some leaseholders/shared owners, depending on the arrangement.
Rebuild cost too low, or cover not in place when required by a mortgage.
Contents
Belongings inside the home, such as furniture, clothes, electronics and non-fixed items.
Homeowners, renters, lodgers and students with belongings to protect.
Underestimating replacement value or missing high-value items.
Combined
Buildings and contents in one policy or package.
Homeowners who need both covers and want one insurer, one renewal and one claims route.
Assuming everything is included without checking limits, excesses and optional extras.

blocks.heading: What does buildings insurance cover?
paragraphs: Buildings insurance covers the physical structure of your home if it is damaged or destroyed by something covered by the policy. This usually includes the walls, roof, floors, ceilings, windows, doors and permanent fixtures such as fitted kitchens and bathrooms.

Policies commonly cover events such as fire, storm, flood, theft, vandalism, burst pipes or escape of water, and subsidence, but the wording differs by insurer. Always check the policy summary and exclusions rather than assuming every event is covered.

Buildings insurance is normally based on the cost of rebuilding the property, not the market value. A home could sell for one amount but cost a different amount to rebuild. If the rebuild cost is too low, you could be underinsured.

blocks.heading: Who usually needs buildings insurance?
items: Freehold homeowners usually arrange their own buildings insurance.
Mortgage lenders usually require buildings insurance as a condition of the mortgage.
Leaseholders may have buildings cover arranged by the freeholder, managing agent or management company, often paid through a service charge.
Tenants usually do not arrange buildings insurance for the property they rent, because this is normally the landlord's responsibility.
Shared owners and owners of flats should check the lease, mortgage paperwork and managing agent documents carefully.

blocks.heading: What does contents insurance cover?
paragraphs: Contents insurance protects the belongings you keep in the home. A simple way to think about it is: if you moved home, would you normally take the item with you? Furniture, clothes, electricals, jewellery, kitchenware, toys and freestanding appliances are usually contents rather than buildings.

Contents insurance can cover loss or damage caused by events such as theft, fire, flood, escape of water or vandalism, depending on the policy. Some policies include accidental damage or cover away from home as standard; others treat these as optional extras.
The biggest mistake is underestimating how much it would cost to replace everything. Go room by room and include everyday items as well as expensive ones. Small items add up quickly.

blocks.heading: Combined buildings and contents insurance
paragraphs: A combined policy puts buildings and contents cover together. This can be simpler for homeowners because there is one insurer, one renewal date and one claims route.

Combined cover can also avoid arguments about whether damage is buildings or contents. For example, a leak might damage flooring, fitted units and personal possessions. If the same insurer covers both sections, the claim may be easier to manage.

Combined is not automatically better or cheaper. Compare the price and cover against separate buildings and contents quotes. Check whether both sections have separate excesses and whether optional extras apply to one section, both sections or neither.

blocks.heading: Common optional extras

cells: Accidental damage
Adds cover for one-off accidents, such as spilling paint on a carpet or damaging a worktop.
Whether it applies to buildings, contents or both.
Personal possessions away from home
Covers items such as phones, jewellery or bags outside the home.
Single-item limits, exclusions and whether worldwide cover is included.

blocks.heading: How to prepare before you compare

items.title: Estimate rebuild cost
items.description: For buildings insurance, use a rebuild-cost estimate rather than the property's sale price. The rebuild cost should include demolition, professional fees and rebuilding work where required.

items.title: Value contents room by room
items.description: For contents insurance, list furniture, electronics, clothes, appliances, jewellery, tools, bikes and everyday items. Use realistic replacement costs.

items.title: Check high-value limits
items.description: Policies often have a single-item limit. Expensive jewellery, watches, art, bikes or technology may need to be listed separately.

items.title: Choose an affordable excess
items.description: A higher excess may reduce the premium but means you pay more towards a claim. Choose an amount you could afford at short notice.

items.title: Review after changes
items.description: Tell your insurer about major changes such as renovations, a lodger, working from home, new valuables, a change of occupancy or leaving the property empty.

blocks.heading: Billgoose Tip
blocks.text: Do not confuse the market value of your home with the rebuild cost. Buildings insurance is about the cost of rebuilding, while contents insurance is about replacing belongings.

blocks.heading: What is usually not covered?
paragraphs: Every policy is different, but common exclusions can include wear and tear, poor maintenance, gradual damage, some types of accidental damage unless added, business use, unoccupied homes beyond a stated period, and items above the single-item limit unless declared.

Flood, storm and subsidence wording can also vary. If your home has a history of flooding, subsidence, structural movement or previous claims, answer questions carefully and check the terms before buying.

blocks.heading: Homeowners, renters and leaseholders: what should you buy?

cells: Freehold homeowner
Buildings and contents, often combined.
Mortgage lender may require buildings cover.
Flat owner / leaseholder
Contents plus check who arranges buildings cover.
Buildings may be covered through freeholder/service charge.
Private renter
Contents cover for belongings.
Landlord normally arranges buildings cover.
Student or lodger
Contents cover, possibly specialist tenant/student cover.
Check cover for shared accommodation and room locks.
Shared owner
Contents plus check lease and housing association/freeholder responsibilities.
Buildings cover arrangement depends on the lease.
Mortgage-free homeowner
Buildings and contents are not usually legally required, but can protect against major financial loss.
Consider whether you could afford repairs or replacement without cover.

blocks.heading: How to compare home insurance quotes properly
paragraphs: Do not compare home insurance on price alone. A cheaper policy can be poor value if it has a low contents limit, high excess, limited escape-of-water cover or excludes the extras you need.

Check buildings and contents limits separately. Compare compulsory and voluntary excesses. Look at single-item limits and whether valuables must be declared. Check accidental damage, personal possessions, bikes and home emergency cover. Confirm alternative accommodation cover if your home becomes uninhabitable. Read exclusions for unoccupied properties, renovations, lodgers and business use. Check flood, storm and subsidence wording if relevant to the property. Compare renewal price with new quotes each year, even though FCA rules restrict renewal pricing practices.

blocks.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
items: Buying contents-only cover when you are responsible for the building.
Assuming a landlord's or freeholder's policy covers your personal belongings.
Using the market value of the property as the rebuild cost.
Underestimating contents because you only count expensive items.
Forgetting garden contents, garages, sheds, bicycles and outbuildings.
Not telling the insurer about renovations or major changes.
Choosing the highest excess just to reduce the premium.
Assuming accidental damage or cover away from home is included.
Letting a policy auto-renew without checking the new terms and limits.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare home insurance?
blocks.text: The right home insurance should match how you live, what you own and who is responsible for the building. Before comparing, gather the property details, rebuild estimate, contents value, claims history, security details and any extras you need.

hero.heading: How Much Broadband Speed Do You Really Need?

blocks.text: How Much Broadband Speed Do You Really Need?

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: Most small households can manage everyday browsing and HD streaming on modest speeds, but busy homes need more headroom. As a rough guide, 30-60 Mbps may suit one or two light users, 60-150 Mbps suits many average households, 150-500 Mbps is better for larger homes with 4K streaming, gaming and home working, and 500 Mbps+ is mainly useful for heavy multi-user households or very large downloads. The right answer depends on how many people are online at the same time, not just the headline speed.

blocks.heading: Broadband speed is about more than one number
paragraphs: Broadband providers usually advertise download speed because it is the easiest number to compare. It affects how quickly you can stream, browse, update devices and download files. But it is not the only thing that determines whether your internet feels fast.

Upload speed, latency, Wi-Fi quality, router position, network congestion and the number of people using the connection at once all matter. A 500 Mbps package can still feel poor if the router is hidden in a cupboard or the signal cannot reach an upstairs office.
This guide explains how to estimate the speed your household actually needs, when it is worth paying for more and when a cheaper package may be enough.

blocks.heading: What Mbps means
paragraphs: Broadband speed is measured in megabits per second, shortened to Mbps or Mbit/s. The higher the number, the more data the connection can move each second. Download speed is used when you watch video, load websites or receive files. Upload speed is used when you send files, back up photos, join video calls or stream your gameplay.

Do not confuse megabits with megabytes. Files are often shown in megabytes or gigabytes, while broadband speeds are shown in megabits. There are eight bits in a byte, so a 1 GB download cannot arrive in one second on a 1 Gbps connection in normal real-world conditions.

Ofcom describes standard broadband as below 30 Mbit/s, superfast broadband as between 30 Mbit/s and 300 Mbit/s, and ultrafast broadband as above 300 Mbit/s. Full fibre services are often capable of much higher and more consistent speeds than older copper-based lines.

blocks.heading: Speed ranges and what they suit

cells: Below 30 Mbps
Basic browsing, email and light streaming for one user.
May struggle with multiple users or 4K video.
30-60 Mbps
One or two people, HD streaming, browsing and occasional video calls.
Limited headroom if several devices are active.
60-150 Mbps
Typical family use, HD/4K streaming, home working and multiple devices.
Wi-Fi quality may become the limiting factor.
Larger households, several 4K streams, gaming updates and frequent downloads.
May be more than light users need.

blocks.heading: How much speed common activities use
paragraphs: Individual activities often need less speed than people expect. The issue is that households do several things at once. One person may be watching 4K TV while someone else is on a video call, a games console downloads an update and phones back up photos.

blocks.heading: Typical speed needed per activity

cells: Browsing and email
Low usage
Responsiveness depends more on Wi-Fi and latency than headline speed.
HD Netflix stream
3-5 Mbps
Netflix recommends 3 Mbps for HD 720p and 5 Mbps for full HD 1080p.
4K Netflix stream
15 Mbps+
Allow extra headroom for other devices and Wi-Fi variation.
Video calls
1-4 Mbps up/down
Zoom lists around 1.2 Mbps for 720p and up to 3.8/3.0 Mbps for 1080p video.
Online gaming
Modest speed, low latency
Ping and stability usually matter more than download speed.
Large downloads
More is better
Faster broadband saves time when downloading games, films or work files.
Cloud backup
Upload matters
A slow upload speed can make backups and sending large files feel sluggish.

blocks.heading: A simple way to estimate your household need

items.title: Count active users
items.description: Focus on how many people are online at the same time, not the total number of devices in the home.

items.title: List the heaviest activities
items.description: 4K streaming, video calls, large downloads, cloud backups and gaming updates are more demanding than browsing.

items.title: Add headroom
items.description: Do not choose a package that only just covers the maths. Wi-Fi conditions and peak-time usage can reduce real-world performance.

items.title: Check upload speed
items.description: Home workers, gamers, content creators and households using cloud backup should not look at download speed alone.

items.title: Compare the actual package terms
items.description: Look for estimated speed, minimum guaranteed speed, contract length, price rises, installation costs and router details.

blocks.heading: What speed do different households need?

cells: One person or a light-use couple
30-60 Mbps can be enough for browsing, email, social media, video calls and HD streaming. Choose more if you watch a lot of 4K, download large files or work from home regularly.
A typical family home
60-150 Mbps is a sensible range for several users, smart TVs, laptops, phones, tablets and occasional gaming. Larger families or homes with multiple 4K streams may benefit from 150 Mbps+.
A home-working household
100-300 Mbps gives more breathing room if video calls, cloud documents and school or entertainment use happen at the same time. Upload speed and connection reliability are especially important.
Gamers

Headline download speed helps with game downloads and updates, but latency and stability matter more during live play. Full fibre or a strong wired connection to the router can make more difference than buying the highest speed.
Heavy users and creators
300-900 Mbps or more may be useful if you regularly upload video, transfer large work files, use cloud storage heavily or have several high-demand users online together.

blocks.heading: Download speed is not the whole story
paragraphs: Upload speed affects anything you send from home: video-call picture quality, file sharing, online backups, smart cameras and broadcasting gameplay. Some broadband packages have much lower upload than download, so check both figures.

Latency, often called ping, is the delay between your device and the service you are using. Lower latency matters for video calls and online gaming. A connection can have a high download speed but still feel poor if latency spikes or the line is unstable.

Many speed problems are actually Wi-Fi problems. Thick walls, distance from the router, interference and old devices can all reduce performance. If speed is good next to the router but poor upstairs, a better router location, mesh system or wired connection may help more than a faster package.

blocks.heading: Billgoose Tip
blocks.text: Before paying for a much faster package, test whether the current problem is the broadband line or the Wi-Fi inside the home. Compare a wired speed test near the router with a Wi-Fi speed test in the room where the problem happens.

blocks.heading: When faster broadband is worth paying for
items: Several people stream, game or work from home at the same time.
You regularly download large games, software updates or work files.
You upload large files, back up photos or create video content.
Your current package is below the minimum guaranteed speed or repeatedly struggles at peak times.
Full fibre is available at a similar price to your current slower package.
You want better reliability and lower latency, not just a higher headline number.

blocks.heading: When you may not need the fastest package
items: Only one or two people use the internet heavily.
Most usage is browsing, email, social media and HD streaming.
The home has poor Wi-Fi coverage that a faster line will not fix by itself.
Devices are old and cannot use very high Wi-Fi speeds.
You rarely download large files or need fast uploads.
The higher-speed deal has a much longer contract or steep mid-contract price rises.

blocks.heading: Check the minimum guaranteed speed
paragraphs: Under Ofcom's broadband speeds code of practice, participating providers should give customers a minimum guaranteed speed for the service. If speeds fall below that level and the provider cannot fix the problem within the required period, customers may have the right to leave without penalty.

This is one reason to read the speed information carefully before switching. The headline advertised speed is useful, but the estimated range and minimum guaranteed speed are more relevant to your address.

blocks.heading: How to compare broadband packages without overpaying

items.title: Start with your postcode
items.description: Availability and speed depend heavily on address, network and technology.

items.title: Choose a realistic speed band
items.description: Use your household size and usage pattern rather than automatically choosing the fastest package.

items.title: Compare total contract cost
items.description: Include monthly price, setup fees, router delivery, discounts, annual increases and contract length.

items.title: Check upload, router and support
items.description: A better router or higher upload speed may matter more than a higher download headline.

items.title: Look for flexibility
items.description: Check cancellation rights, minimum guaranteed speed and what happens if the service underperforms.

blocks.heading: Ready to find a broadband speed that fits?
blocks.text: A good broadband deal is not always the fastest one. It is the package that gives your household enough speed, reliable Wi-Fi, fair contract terms and a price that makes sense.
blocks.highlightText: Enter your postcode, choose how your household uses the internet and compare broadband packages by speed, price, contract length and key terms. The aim is to find enough speed without paying for capacity you will not use.

hero.heading: How to Choose the Right Mobile Data Allowance

image.alt: Person using mobile phone at a train station

blocks.text: How to Choose the Right Mobile Data Allowance

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: Start with your actual usage, not the data allowance a network wants to sell you. Check the last three months of mobile data use in your phone settings or mobile account, then choose an allowance slightly above your normal peak month. Light users may only need 1-5GB, moderate users often sit around 10-30GB, and heavy streamers, hotspot users or frequent travellers may need 50GB, 100GB or unlimited. Also check coverage, roaming, speed limits and price rises before choosing.

blocks.heading: Why data allowance matters
paragraphs: Mobile data is what your phone uses when it is not connected to Wi-Fi. It powers maps, messaging, browsing, music, video, app updates, social media, video calls and tethering a laptop or tablet.
Choosing too little data can mean running out, buying expensive add-ons or constantly worrying about usage. Choosing too much can mean paying every month for a safety cushion you rarely use.

The best mobile deal is not always the one with the biggest allowance. It is the one that gives you enough data, good coverage in the places you actually go, fair roaming terms and a price that stays competitive over the contract.

blocks.heading: Step one: check your actual data use

items.title: Check your phone settings
items.description: On iPhone, check Mobile Service / Cellular data usage. On Android, check Network & Internet or Connections / Data usage. Reset the counter monthly if it is not already aligned to your billing cycle.

items.title: Check your provider account
items.description: Your network account or app usually shows recent monthly usage, remaining allowance and any add-ons you bought.

items.title: Look at at least three months
items.description: One quiet month can be misleading. Use your highest normal month as the starting point.

items.title: Allow for lifestyle changes
items.description: New commute, more travel, less Wi-Fi, a new job, video calls or a child using hotspot data can all change your needs.

items.title: Add a sensible buffer
items.description: If you normally use 8GB, a 10GB or 12GB plan may be enough. If you sometimes use 18GB, a 20GB or 30GB plan may feel safer.

blocks.heading: What different data allowances are usually suitable for

cells: 1-3GB
Very light users: messaging, email, maps and occasional browsing.
Easy to exceed with video, social media reels or app downloads.
Light to moderate users with regular Wi-Fi at home and work.
May feel tight if you stream video or commute frequently.
Typical smartphone users who browse, stream music, use maps and watch some short video.
Check whether heavy video days push you above the allowance.
Heavy users, frequent social video, hotspot use, travel or limited home Wi-Fi.
Can be overkill if your phone spends most of the day on Wi-Fi.
Unlimited
Very heavy users, frequent tethering, streaming away from Wi-Fi or households replacing fixed broadband temporarily.
Check fair-use rules, speed caps, roaming limits and whether unlimited is genuinely needed.

blocks.heading: What uses the most mobile data?

cells: Short messages and email
Low data use for text, higher if sending photos or files.
Use Wi-Fi for large attachments.
Maps and navigation
Usually moderate, but can add up on long trips.
Download offline maps where available.
Music and podcasts
Moderate if streamed daily.
Download playlists and podcasts on Wi-Fi.
Social media
Can be high because of autoplay video and reels.
Turn off autoplay or use data saver modes.
Video streaming
High and highly dependent on quality settings.
Use Wi-Fi, download shows in advance or lower quality.
Video calls
Can be high and needs a stable connection.
Use Wi-Fi where possible and enable data-saving settings.
Hotspot / tethering
Can use a lot quickly because laptops update and stream like home broadband.
Avoid large downloads and cloud backups on hotspot.

blocks.heading: Coverage matters as much as data
paragraphs: A large data allowance is only useful if the network works where you need it. Check coverage at home, work, school, regular travel routes and places where you often use your phone indoors.

Ofcom provides a mobile coverage checker called Map Your Mobile. It shows 4G and 5G signal information by postcode, including whether coverage is likely indoors or outdoors and whether the signal may be good or variable.

blocks.heading: Coverage Before Allowance
blocks.text: A cheap 100GB plan on a weak network may be worse value than a smaller allowance on a network that works reliably where you live and travel.

blocks.heading: Do you really need unlimited data?
paragraphs: Unlimited data can be good value for the right user. It can remove bill anxiety and suit people who stream away from Wi-Fi, travel frequently, use hotspot data or have unreliable fixed broadband.

However, unlimited is not automatically the best deal. Check whether the plan has fair-use policies, speed management, roaming limits, tethering restrictions or a higher price after an introductory period. If your real monthly use is 12GB, a well-priced 20GB or 30GB plan may be better value.

blocks.heading: Watch out for roaming and fair-use limits
paragraphs: Roaming terms vary by provider and plan. Some UK mobile plans include roaming in certain destinations, some charge daily fees, and some include a fair-use limit that is lower than your UK data allowance.

If you travel, do not just compare UK data. Check destination coverage, roaming cost per day, included countries, fair-use caps, speed restrictions and what happens if you exceed the roaming allowance.

blocks.heading: SIM-only, phone contract or family plan?

cells: SIM-only
People who already have a handset or want flexibility.
Often the easiest way to adjust data up or down.
Phone contract
People who want a new handset spread across monthly payments.
Avoid overbuying data just because the handset deal looks attractive.
Family or shared plan
Households with multiple users.
Check whether data is shared, capped, rolled over or charged separately.
PAYG or rolling monthly
Light users, children, second phones or uncertain usage.
Useful while you learn how much data you actually need.

blocks.heading: Price rises and contract length
paragraphs: For new telecoms contracts, Ofcom rules require any contractually agreed price rises to be shown upfront in pounds and pence at the point of sale. That matters when comparing data allowances because a slightly cheaper plan today may not stay cheaper across the full contract.
Compare the total contract cost, not only the first monthly price. Check the minimum term, annual price rise wording, upgrade options, downgrade restrictions and what it costs to leave early.

blocks.heading: How to reduce mobile data use without feeling restricted
items: Download video, music, podcasts and maps on Wi-Fi before travelling.
Turn off autoplay video in social media apps where possible.
Use data saver mode in streaming, maps and video-call apps.
Restrict app updates, cloud photo backup and system downloads to Wi-Fi.
Set a monthly data warning or limit on your phone.
Check which apps use the most background data and restrict the worst offenders.
Use Wi-Fi calling and trusted Wi-Fi networks where appropriate.
Be careful with hotspot use, especially with laptops and tablets.

blocks.heading: Simple rule of thumb
paragraphs: If you use less than half your allowance for three months in a row, compare smaller plans. If you use more than 80-90% most months, compare the next allowance up before you get caught by add-on charges.

blocks.heading: Switching mobile provider
paragraphs: If you find a better plan, switching is usually straightforward. Ofcom says you can text PAC to 65075 if you want to keep your existing number, or STAC to 75075 if you want a new number. The switching code is valid for 30 days, and the provider response must include important information such as early termination charges.
Before switching, check coverage, contract end date, handset payments, roaming, voicemail, Wi-Fi calling and any linked discounts from broadband or family plans.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare mobile plans?
blocks.text: The right data allowance should feel comfortable without being wasteful. Start with your actual usage, add a sensible buffer, then compare networks, contract length, roaming, price rises and total cost.
blocks.highlightText: Use Billgoose to compare SIM-only and mobile deals by data allowance, monthly cost, contract length, network and key terms. Choose enough data for real life — not the largest number on the page.

hero.heading: How to Compare Car Insurance Without Choosing the Wrong Cover

blocks.text: How to Compare Car Insurance Without Choosing the Wrong Cover

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: Do not choose car insurance by price alone. Start with the level of cover you need, then compare excesses, exclusions, no-claims rules, named drivers, mileage, use class, courtesy car, windscreen cover, legal expenses and payment terms. A cheaper policy can become expensive if it leaves out the protection you expected or makes it difficult to claim when something goes wrong.

blocks.heading: Why the cheapest quote can be the wrong quote
paragraphs: Car insurance is a legal requirement if you use a vehicle on roads or in public places. If the vehicle is kept off the road and declared SORN, it does not need to be insured; otherwise continuous insurance enforcement rules mean the registered keeper must keep it insured.

That legal requirement can make car insurance feel like a box to tick. But the policy you choose affects what happens after an accident, theft, fire, vandalism, windscreen damage, injury claim or dispute.

The aim is not to buy the most expensive policy. The aim is to avoid paying for the wrong policy. Compare the cover as carefully as the price, and make sure the quote reflects how the car is actually used.

blocks.heading: The three main levels of car insurance cover

cells: Third party
The legal minimum. Covers injury to other people and damage to other people's property caused by you.
It does not normally cover repairs to your own car if the accident is your fault.
Third party, fire and theft
Third party cover plus cover if your car is stolen or damaged by fire.
It still may not cover your own car for accident damage caused by you.
Comprehensive
Includes third party, fire and theft plus cover for damage to your own car, subject to policy terms.
Benefits vary. Courtesy car, windscreen, legal expenses and belongings cover may have limits or optional extras.

blocks.note: Comprehensive cover is not always the most expensive option, so it is worth comparing all suitable cover levels rather than assuming a lower level will automatically cost less.

blocks.heading: Your car insurance comparison checklist

items.title: Choose the right cover level
items.description: Decide whether third-party, third-party fire and theft or comprehensive cover is suitable. Do not rely on price alone.

items.title: Check the excess
items.description: Look at both compulsory and voluntary excess. A high excess can reduce the premium but may make smaller claims unaffordable.

items.title: Compare key extras
items.description: Check windscreen cover, courtesy car, legal expenses, personal accident, breakdown cover and personal belongings limits.

items.title: Use accurate details
items.description: Mileage, address, occupation, parking location, modifications, claims history and driving convictions must be accurate.

items.title: Check who can drive
items.description: Named-driver, any-driver and driving-other-cars cover can be restricted. Do not assume someone is covered.

items.title: Review no-claims rules
items.description: Check whether your no-claims discount is protected, how many claims are allowed and what still affects the premium.

items.title: Look at payment terms
items.description: Monthly payment is often a credit agreement and can cost more than paying annually.

items.title: Read the exclusions
items.description: Every policy has exclusions. Look for restrictions that would matter to your household before you buy.

blocks.heading: Do not compare policies unless the details match
paragraphs: A comparison is only useful if each quote is based on the same information. Changing details to get a cheaper price can create problems at claim time and may invalidate cover.

Pay particular attention to annual mileage, overnight parking, main driver, named drivers, business use, modifications and how the car is financed. If the quote asks whether the car is used for commuting, include commuting if you drive to one regular place of work.

blocks.heading: Avoid Fronting
blocks.text: The main driver should be the person who drives the car most. Putting a more experienced person as the main driver when a younger or higher-risk driver actually uses the car most can be treated as fronting and can cause serious issues with the policy.

blocks.heading: Excess: cheap premium, expensive claim?
paragraphs: The excess is the amount you pay towards a claim. There may be a compulsory excess set by the insurer and a voluntary excess chosen by you.

Increasing voluntary excess can reduce the premium, but only choose an excess you could comfortably pay. If the total excess is £700, a claim for a £900 repair may not feel worthwhile, and you could still affect your claims history.

blocks.heading: Quick Excess Test
blocks.text: Ask: if I had an accident tomorrow, could I pay this excess without borrowing? If the answer is no, the policy may be too risky even if the monthly premium looks attractive.

blocks.heading: Key extras explained

cells: Courtesy car
Keeps you mobile while your car is repaired after an insured claim.
Is it guaranteed, like-for-like, or only available if repairers are used?
Windscreen cover
Can reduce the cost of repairing or replacing glass.
What is the excess and does it affect no claims?
Legal expenses
Can help recover uninsured losses after a non-fault accident.
What limit applies and when can it be used?
Protected no claims
Can protect the discount after limited claims.
It protects the discount, not necessarily the whole premium.
Breakdown cover
Useful if you do not already have cover elsewhere.
Check roadside, home start, recovery and onward travel levels.
Personal belongings
Covers items stolen from or damaged in the car.
Limits can be low and exclusions common.
Driving abroad
Useful for trips to Europe or beyond.
Check countries, days covered and level of cover abroad.

blocks.heading: No-claims discount: important, but not magic
paragraphs: A no-claims discount can make a large difference to the price, but the rules vary by insurer. Some insurers offer protected no-claims discount, which may allow a limited number of claims without reducing the discount.

Protection does not mean your premium cannot rise after a claim. It usually protects the discount percentage, while the underlying premium can still change because the insurer may view the risk differently.
When comparing, check whether no-claims protection is included, optional or unavailable, and how many claims are allowed before the protection is affected.

blocks.heading: Automatic renewal and renewal pricing
paragraphs: The FCA introduced rules so that renewing home and motor insurance customers should not be quoted a renewal price that is higher than the equivalent new-customer price through the same channel.

That does not mean your renewal is automatically the cheapest option in the market. It simply means you should still compare. Your circumstances, the insurer's pricing, claims inflation, repair costs and market competition can all affect the renewal price.
If your policy auto-renews, check the renewal notice, cancellation deadline and payment method. Do not rely on the insurer to choose the best deal for you.

blocks.heading: Telematics, black box and pay-per-mile policies
paragraphs: Telematics policies can suit new drivers, low-mileage drivers or people who are confident their driving habits will score well. They may monitor mileage, time of day, speed, braking, acceleration and location.

Before choosing one, check curfews, mileage limits, installation requirements, data use, cancellation charges and what happens if your driving score falls. Pay-per-mile policies can be useful for low-mileage drivers, but they need careful comparison against standard annual policies.

blocks.heading: A better way to compare car insurance

items.title: Set your must-haves
items.description: For example: comprehensive cover, affordable excess, commuting, protected no claims and windscreen cover.

items.title: Run like-for-like quotes
items.description: Keep driver, car, mileage, address, parking and cover details consistent.

items.title: Shortlist by value, not just price
items.description: Remove policies that miss important cover or include unacceptable exclusions.

items.title: Read the policy summary
items.description: Check the Insurance Product Information Document, excesses, exclusions and cancellation fees.

items.title: Save the evidence
items.description: Keep the quote, policy summary, statement of fact and renewal date for future comparison.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare car insurance?
blocks.text: Good car insurance comparison is about balance: the right cover, a fair excess, accurate details and a price that makes sense. A slightly more expensive policy can be better value if it protects you from a much bigger problem later.
