hero.heading: How to Compare Energy Deals Without Getting Confused

blocks.text: How to Compare Energy Deals Without Getting Confused

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: To compare energy deals properly, use your annual gas and electricity consumption where possible, compare the total estimated yearly cost rather than the monthly direct debit alone, check whether the tariff is fixed or variable, review standing charges and unit rates, and look for exit fees or special conditions. The cheapest-looking deal is not always the best fit for your home.

blocks.heading: Energy comparison does not need to be complicated
paragraphs: Energy tariffs can look confusing because suppliers present several numbers at once: estimated annual cost, monthly direct debit, unit rates, standing charges, contract length and possible exit fees. The good news is that you do not need to become an energy-market expert to make a sensible choice.

A useful comparison answers three questions: what could the tariff cost for your actual usage, how could that price change, and what commitments or restrictions come with it? Once you focus on those points, it becomes much easier to separate a genuinely suitable deal from one that simply has an attractive headline.
This guide explains the information to collect, the figures to compare and the checks to make before you switch.

blocks.heading: Before you compare: collect the right information

cells: Your postcode and address
Energy prices and available tariffs can vary by region.
Your current supplier and tariff
This helps establish what you are comparing against.
Your annual electricity and gas consumption
Look for figures shown in kilowatt-hours (kWh). Using actual consumption is usually more accurate than choosing a broad household estimate.
How you pay
For example, monthly direct debit, payment on receipt of bill or prepayment.
Your meter type
This might include a standard meter, prepayment meter, Economy 7 or another time-of-use arrangement.
Your tariff end date and exit fee
A fixed tariff may charge you for leaving early, although terms vary.

blocks.heading: The five figures that matter most

items.title: Estimated annual cost
items.description: This is usually the simplest starting point because it combines the tariff's unit rates, standing charges and your estimated consumption. Compare annual costs on the same usage assumptions. A low monthly direct debit is not proof that the tariff is cheaper.

items.title: Unit rates
items.description: The unit rate is the amount charged for each kilowatt-hour of gas or electricity you use. A household that uses more energy will be affected more by the unit rate than a household with very low consumption.

items.title: Standing charges
items.description: The standing charge is a daily amount payable even when little or no energy is used. Lower-use households should pay particular attention to standing charges because they make up a larger proportion of the total bill.

items.title: Contract length and price type
items.description: A fixed tariff normally fixes the unit rates and standing charges for an agreed period; it does not fix your total bill. Ofgem's price cap limits the unit rates and standing charges suppliers can charge customers on standard variable tariffs, but it is not a cap on the total bill.

items.title: Exit fees and other conditions
items.description: Check whether you would pay a fee for leaving a fixed deal early, whether the tariff requires a smart meter or particular payment method, and whether any reward or discount is temporary.

blocks.heading: Billgoose Tip
blocks.text: Do not rank tariffs by one number in isolation. Compare the estimated annual cost, then use the unit rates, standing charges, contract terms and service features to decide whether the deal suits you.

blocks.heading: Fixed or variable: which should you choose?
columns: A fixed tariff may suit you if...
A variable tariff may suit you if...

cells: Budget certainty
You prefer more certainty about the rates for a set period.
You can accept rates changing.
Flexibility
You are comfortable committing, subject to the tariff terms.
You want fewer barriers to changing tariff.
Market movement
You value protection from potential rate increases.
You are willing to accept increases in return for flexibility or possible reductions.

blocks.heading: How to compare energy deals step by step

items.title: Enter your postcode
items.description: This identifies your region and available supply address.

items.title: Choose your address
items.description: Select the correct property so the comparison uses the right supply information.

items.title: Add your current tariff and usage
items.description: Use annual kWh figures when available. Otherwise provide the best estimate you can.

items.title: Review the results consistently
items.description: Keep the same usage and payment assumptions across every tariff.

items.title: Filter for what matters
items.description: For example: fixed or variable, tariff length, green energy claims, payment method, meter compatibility and exit fees.

items.title: Open the tariff details
items.description: Read the key terms, not only the headline saving.

items.title: Choose and complete the switch
items.description: Provide the required information and keep a copy of the confirmation.

blocks.heading: What happens when you switch?
paragraphs: Your energy supply should not be interrupted. The gas and electricity continue through the same pipes, wires and meters; the company that bills you changes. Ofgem says a supplier switch should take up to five working days, although you can ask for a later date. Domestic customers also normally receive a 14-day cooling-off period.

Your old supplier should produce a final bill. Take or submit an accurate meter reading when requested, keep your confirmation emails and check any credit balance is returned. If you use a smart meter, check whether it will continue operating in smart mode with the new tariff or supplier.

blocks.heading: Common energy comparison mistakes
items: Comparing the monthly direct debit instead of the total estimated cost.
Using different consumption figures for different tariffs.
Ignoring standing charges because the unit rate looks low.
Assuming a fixed tariff fixes the total bill rather than the rates.
Forgetting to check an existing exit fee.
Choosing a tariff that is incompatible with the meter or payment method.
Treating an estimated saving as guaranteed.
Ignoring customer service, billing and support arrangements.

blocks.heading: When switching might need extra care
paragraphs: Some circumstances require additional checks. You might still be able to switch if you owe money, but the rules depend on factors such as when the debt arose and whether you use a prepayment meter. Tenants who pay the supplier directly can generally choose their own supplier or tariff. If your existing supplier has failed, Ofgem advises customers to wait while a new supplier is appointed rather than trying to switch immediately.
Seek impartial help if you are struggling to pay, have been switched without permission, or are unsure how a tariff affects a vulnerable household member.

hero.heading: How to Read Your Energy Bill in Plain English

blocks.text: How to Read Your Energy Bill in Plain English

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: Your energy bill shows how much gas and electricity you used, the rates charged, the daily standing charges, your payments and whether the account is in credit or debit. Start by checking the billing period, whether the readings are actual or estimated, the unit rates in pence per kilowatt-hour, and the balance carried forward. These details help you spot errors and compare tariffs accurately.

blocks.heading: Why energy bills feel more complicated than they are
paragraphs: Energy bills contain a lot of information because they combine consumption, tariff pricing, meter readings, payments and account balances. Suppliers also use slightly different layouts, so the same information may appear under different headings.

The useful approach is to read the bill in a set order rather than starting with the amount due. First identify the period covered, then check the meter readings and usage, review the rates and standing charges, and finally reconcile the account balance and payments.

Once you know where these figures appear, your bill becomes a practical tool. It can help you monitor energy use, challenge an inaccurate charge and provide the information needed for a more accurate tariff comparison.

blocks.heading: Step 1: Check the billing period

items.title: Confirm the dates
items.description: The amount charged only makes sense when you know the period it covers. A bill spanning a cold winter month may be much higher than one covering summer, particularly for homes with gas heating.

items.title: Look for unusual lengths
items.description: A longer bill may include a correction, a delayed statement or charges brought forward from an earlier estimate. If the dates overlap with a previous bill, contact the supplier and ask for an explanation.

blocks.heading: Step 2: Check whether meter readings are actual or estimated
paragraphs: Suppliers use meter readings to calculate the difference between the energy recorded at the beginning and end of the billing period. The bill may mark readings as actual, customer readings, smart-meter readings or estimates.

If a supplier does not receive a reading, it may estimate your usage. An estimated bill can be too high or too low. Citizens Advice recommends submitting regular readings to keep bills accurate. If an estimated bill looks wrong, take a current reading and send it to the supplier so the account can be updated.

blocks.heading: Estimated does not mean incorrect — but it does mean check
blocks.text: An estimate may be reasonable, but it should be compared with the meter. A bill that is repeatedly underestimated can leave you with a larger catch-up charge later.

blocks.heading: Step 3: Understand kilowatt-hours
paragraphs: Energy use is charged in kilowatt-hours, usually written as kWh. Electricity meters generally record electricity in kWh. Gas meters may record cubic metres or cubic feet, which the supplier converts into kWh using a calculation shown on the bill.

For comparison purposes, the most useful figure is your annual gas and electricity use in kWh. It allows different tariffs to estimate costs using the same consumption, which is more reliable than choosing a vague low, medium or high household profile.

blocks.heading: Steps 4 and 5: Find the unit rate and standing charge
paragraphs: The unit rate is the amount charged for each kWh used. It is normally shown in pence per kWh. Gas and electricity have separate rates, and some electricity tariffs use more than one rate. For example, an Economy 7 or time-of-use tariff may show a daytime rate and a cheaper overnight rate.
The standing charge is a daily fee payable even if no energy is used. A bill normally calculates it by multiplying the daily standing charge by the number of days in the billing period.

Standing charges matter when comparing tariffs. A lower unit rate can be offset by a higher daily charge, particularly in a low-use household. Citizens Advice describes a tariff as including both the rate paid for energy and the daily standing charge.

blocks.heading: Step 6: Understand the difference between the bill and the direct debit
paragraphs: The bill is the cost of the energy and charges applied to your account. The direct debit is the amount collected as a payment. They are related, but they are not the same thing.

Monthly direct debits are usually based on an estimate of annual use, spread across the year. This can create credit during lower-use months and use that credit during winter. A supplier may change the direct debit if actual use, prices or the account balance differ from the estimate.

blocks.heading: Energy charge vs direct debit payment

cells: Based on usage, unit rates and standing charges.
A payment towards the running account balance.
Can vary with actual consumption.
May be kept similar each month to smooth seasonal costs.
Appears as a new charge on the account.
Appears as money paid into the account.

blocks.heading: Step 7: Work out whether you are in credit or debit
paragraphs: A credit balance generally means you have paid more into the account than the charges currently applied. A debit balance means the charges are higher than the payments received.

A small seasonal credit is not automatically a problem, particularly before winter. But a large or persistent credit may justify asking the supplier to review your direct debit or refund some of the balance. Citizens Advice notes that direct-debit customers may build credit because monthly payments are based on estimated annual use.
Do not cancel a direct debit solely because the account is in credit. First check upcoming usage, recent price changes and whether the bill is based on accurate readings.

blocks.heading: Step 8: Check the tariff details
paragraphs: The bill or annual statement should identify your tariff and may show whether it is fixed or variable, its end date, the payment method and any exit fee. This information is essential when deciding whether to switch.

If a fixed tariff is ending, note the date and begin comparing before the contract expires. If you are on a standard variable tariff, the rates may be covered by Ofgem's price cap. The cap limits unit rates and standing charges for eligible default tariffs; it does not cap the total bill.

blocks.heading: Step 9: Look for the estimated annual consumption and cost
paragraphs: Many bills show estimated annual consumption, an estimated annual cost or both. These figures are useful reference points, but they depend on past use, current tariff rates and supplier assumptions.
Use the annual kWh figures when comparing tariffs. If the annual consumption appears unrealistic, check whether recent bills have been estimated or whether your household circumstances have changed.

blocks.heading: Electricity example
blocks.text: The bill covers 30 days. The household used 240 kWh. The unit rate is 25p per kWh, so the usage charge is £60. The standing charge is 55p per day, adding £16.50. Before VAT, discounts or account adjustments, the electricity charge is £76.50. The direct debit paid during the month is then applied to the account balance.

blocks.heading: Quick bill-check checklist

items.title: Confirm the dates
items.description: Make sure the billing period is clear and does not unexpectedly overlap another statement.

items.title: Check the readings
items.description: Compare the closing reading on the bill with the meter and note whether it is actual or estimated.

items.title: Check the maths
items.description: Multiply usage by the unit rate and the number of days by the standing charge.

items.title: Reconcile payments
items.description: Confirm that direct debits, card payments or credits appear in the account summary.

items.title: Review the tariff
items.description: Record the tariff name, annual kWh use, end date and exit fee for comparison.

blocks.heading: Signs that something may be wrong
items: The meter reading on the bill is significantly higher than the meter itself.
A bill is based on estimates even though recent readings were submitted.
The billing period overlaps an earlier bill.
The unit rate or standing charge does not match the tariff information.
A payment is missing from the account summary.
The bill uses the wrong meter serial number or address.
Usage rises sharply without an obvious change in the household.
A large balance appears after months without an accurate bill.

blocks.heading: What to do if the bill looks too high
paragraphs: Take a meter reading and compare it with the reading used on the bill. Check the dates, rates and payment history. If the bill is estimated, submit the reading and ask the supplier for an updated statement.

If the meter reading and rates are correct, consider whether usage has genuinely changed. Heating, electric vehicles, faulty appliances, immersion heaters and additional occupants can all affect consumption.

Contact the supplier if you cannot explain the charge. Keep copies of bills, readings and correspondence. If you are struggling to pay, contact the supplier promptly and seek independent help rather than ignoring the bill.

blocks.heading: What is back billing?
paragraphs: Back billing is when a supplier charges for energy used in an earlier period. Citizens Advice explains that protections can limit charging for energy used more than 12 months ago where the supplier failed to bill correctly and the customer did not obstruct accurate billing.
The rules depend on the circumstances. If you receive a large historic charge, ask the supplier for a full breakdown and check whether back-billing protections apply.

blocks.text: Have your latest bill to hand. Billgoose can use the tariff and annual-consumption information to help you compare current energy deals on a like-for-like basis.

blocks.highlightText: Your bill contains the information needed for a meaningful energy comparison: postcode, current supplier, tariff name, annual gas and electricity consumption, payment method, tariff end date and exit fee. Enter the annual kWh figures rather than relying on a generic estimate.

hero.heading: How to Reduce Your Car Insurance Premium Legally

blocks.text: How to Reduce Your Car Insurance Premium Legally

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: You can reduce car insurance legally by shopping around before renewal, giving accurate information, choosing the right cover level, setting a sensible voluntary excess, protecting and building your no-claims discount, avoiding unnecessary extras, paying annually if affordable, considering telematics or pay-by-mile cover, and choosing a car that is cheaper to insure. Do not lie about the main driver, address, mileage, job, modifications or how the car is used. A cheaper premium is not worth invalid insurance.

blocks.heading: Why "legally" matters
paragraphs: Car insurance is priced on risk. Insurers look at details such as your car, address, age, driving history, mileage, job, claims record, named drivers and how the vehicle is used. Small changes can affect the premium, but they must be true.

There is a difference between finding a better deal and misrepresenting the risk. If you give false or misleading information, the insurer may cancel the policy, refuse a claim or treat the policy as if it never existed. That can leave you personally responsible for costs and make future insurance harder to arrange.
The aim is simple: reduce unnecessary cost while keeping cover that still works if you need to claim.

blocks.heading: Legal Baseline
blocks.text: You must have motor insurance if you use your vehicle on roads or in public places. A vehicle kept off the road does not need insurance only if it is declared SORN and kept off the road.

blocks.heading: Your legal premium-reduction checklist

items.title: Compare before renewal
items.description: Do not accept a renewal price without checking the market. Compare like-for-like cover, not just the cheapest monthly figure.

items.title: Use accurate details
items.description: Check your address, occupation, use class, annual mileage, parking, claims, convictions and modifications are all correct.

items.title: Choose the right cover level
items.description: Compare comprehensive, third party fire and theft, and third party only. Comprehensive can sometimes be cheaper than more limited cover.

items.title: Set a sensible voluntary excess
items.description: A higher voluntary excess can reduce the premium, but only choose an amount you could afford if you had to claim.

items.title: Protect your no-claims discount wisely
items.description: A no-claims discount can be valuable. Compare the cost of protecting it with the potential benefit.

items.title: Review optional extras
items.description: Remove extras you do not need, such as duplicate breakdown cover, legal expenses, courtesy car upgrade or key cover.

items.title: Consider telematics or pay-by-mile
items.description: Black box, app-based or low-mileage policies can suit careful drivers or people who drive less.

items.title: Pay annually if affordable
items.description: Monthly payments can include credit charges or interest. Compare the total cost, not just the monthly amount.

items.title: Keep the car secure
items.description: Parking, alarms, immobilisers and avoiding unnecessary modifications can affect price and acceptance.

items.title: Avoid fronting
items.description: Do not name a lower-risk person as the main driver if someone else actually uses the car most. That can be treated as insurance fraud.

blocks.heading: What usually reduces the price, and what to watch for

cells: Shop around
Different insurers price the same risk differently.
Compare cover, excess and add-ons, not just the headline premium.
Increase voluntary excess
You take on more of the claim cost yourself.
Do not set an excess you could not afford.
Reduce mileage if accurate
Lower mileage can reduce exposure to risk.
Do not understate mileage. Update the insurer if usage changes.
Pay annually
Avoids monthly credit charges where they apply.
Only do this if it does not create cash-flow problems.
Add a named driver
An experienced genuine named driver may reduce risk.
Never use this to disguise the real main driver.
Remove extras
Stops paying for duplicate or unwanted benefits.
Do not remove cover you would genuinely need after a claim.
Telematics
Rewards safer or lower-risk driving patterns.
Check data use, curfews, scoring and cancellation terms.
Choose a lower-risk car
Repairs, performance and theft risk affect price.
Check insurance cost before buying or modifying a car.

blocks.heading: 1. Shop around before your renewal date
paragraphs: Your renewal price is not automatically the best available price. FCA rules introduced from 2022 were designed to stop insurers charging renewing home and motor customers more than an equivalent new customer through the same channel, but that does not mean every insurer will quote the same price or that your current provider will be cheapest.

Compare at least a few weeks before your renewal date. Make sure each quote uses the same details, cover level, excess, add-ons and payment method. If your current insurer is more expensive, ask whether they can match or improve the price, but get any offer confirmed before agreeing.

blocks.heading: 2. Give accurate mileage and use class
paragraphs: Annual mileage matters because it tells the insurer how much the car is likely to be on the road. If you now work from home, use public transport more, or no longer commute, your expected mileage may have fallen. Updating it honestly can help.

The same applies to use class. Social, domestic and pleasure use is different from commuting or business use. Choose the class that matches how the car is actually used. The cheapest option is not useful if it leaves the policy wrong.

blocks.heading: 3. Choose cover level by value, not assumption
paragraphs: Many drivers assume third party only is always cheapest because it offers less cover. In practice, insurers price based on claims experience and risk, so comprehensive cover can sometimes be cheaper than more limited cover.

Compare all suitable cover levels before choosing. Third party only may meet the minimum legal requirement for driving on public roads, but it will not pay to repair or replace your own car after an at-fault accident.

blocks.heading: 4. Set the excess carefully
paragraphs: The excess is the amount you contribute towards a claim. Policies usually include a compulsory excess set by the insurer and may allow you to choose an additional voluntary excess.

A higher voluntary excess can reduce the premium because you take on more of the risk. But if the total excess becomes too high, the policy may be less useful for smaller claims. Choose an amount you could pay without borrowing if something happened.

blocks.heading: 5. Build and protect your no-claims discount
paragraphs: A no-claims discount can make a significant difference to the premium. It rewards claim-free driving history, although the size of the discount and how it is applied varies by insurer.

If you have built up a discount, compare the cost of protecting it. Protection does not stop the underlying premium from changing after a claim, but it may preserve the discount percentage according to the policy terms.

blocks.heading: 6. Be careful with named drivers
paragraphs: Adding a genuine named driver can sometimes reduce the premium, especially if they are experienced and will occasionally use the car. It can also increase the price if the additional driver is higher risk.

The main driver must be the person who uses the car most. Naming a parent or partner as the main driver when a younger or higher-risk person is the real main driver is commonly known as fronting. It can invalidate cover and may be treated as fraud.

blocks.heading: 7. Consider telematics, low-mileage or pay-by-mile cover
paragraphs: Telematics policies use a black box, plug-in device or app to monitor driving behaviour. They can suit newer drivers, careful drivers or people who are comfortable sharing driving data in return for a potentially lower price.

Low-mileage or pay-by-mile policies can also be worth checking if you do not drive often. Read the terms carefully, including mileage caps, device requirements, admin fees, data use and what happens if your mileage increases.

blocks.heading: 8. Remove extras you do not need
paragraphs: Optional extras can be useful, but they can also duplicate cover you already have. Check breakdown cover, legal expenses, personal accident, key cover, courtesy car, protected no-claims and enhanced windscreen cover separately.
Do not remove an extra just to make the quote cheaper if you would genuinely rely on it. The right approach is to remove duplication and avoid paying for benefits that do not fit your situation.

blocks.heading: 9. Pay annually if it makes financial sense
paragraphs: Paying monthly can be convenient, but it often means the insurer or finance provider is extending credit. That can make the total amount payable higher than a single annual payment.
Compare the annual premium against the total cost of monthly instalments. If paying annually would cause financial pressure, it may not be the right choice, but it is worth knowing the difference.

blocks.heading: 10. Check the car before you buy or modify it
paragraphs: The vehicle itself has a major effect on insurance. A powerful, expensive, rare or heavily modified car can cost more to repair or replace, and may attract higher premiums.

Before buying a car, run insurance quotes for the exact registration or model. If you modify the vehicle, tell the insurer. Even cosmetic changes can matter if they alter value, theft risk or repair cost.

blocks.heading: Things that are not worth the risk
items: Using a different address because it is cheaper.
Understating mileage when you know you will drive more.
Leaving commuting or business use off the policy when you need it.
Failing to disclose claims, accidents or motoring convictions when asked.
Failing to disclose modifications.
Naming someone else as the main driver when they are not.
Choosing an excess so high that you could not realistically claim.
Buying the cheapest policy without checking exclusions and compulsory excesses.

blocks.heading: A simple renewal checklist

items.title: Open your renewal notice
items.description: Write down the annual price, monthly total, cover level, excess and optional extras.

items.title: Check your details
items.description: Update mileage, job, usage, parking, named drivers and vehicle details if they have changed.

items.title: Run fresh quotes
items.description: Compare like-for-like and also test sensible alternatives such as different excess levels or cover types.

items.title: Challenge the renewal
items.description: Ask your insurer whether they can improve the price or match equivalent cover.

items.title: Save the evidence
items.description: Keep quote references, policy documents and cancellation confirmation from the old insurer.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare car insurance?
blocks.text: Reducing car insurance is not about finding loopholes. It is about making sure your quote reflects your real risk, your real cover needs and the best available price for the policy you actually want.

hero.heading: Pet Insurance Explained: What Is and Isn't Usually Covered?

image.alt: Dog and cat at the vet

blocks.text: Pet Insurance Explained: What Is and Isn't Usually Covered?

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: Pet insurance can help with unexpected vet bills, but it does not cover everything. Policies usually focus on illness and injury treatment, with limits depending on the type of cover. Routine costs such as vaccinations, neutering, flea and worm treatment, grooming and most pre-existing conditions are usually not covered. The most important comparison points are the policy type, annual or condition limit, excess, co-payment, exclusions, your pet's age and whether long-term conditions remain covered when the policy renews.

blocks.heading: Why pet insurance can be confusing
paragraphs: Pet insurance looks simple at first: you pay a monthly or annual premium and the insurer helps with eligible vet bills. In practice, policies can work very differently.

Two policies with similar prices may offer very different protection. One may provide a high annual vet-fee limit that renews each year, while another may only cover a condition for 12 months or up to a fixed amount. That difference matters if your pet develops a long-term condition.

This guide explains the main types of pet insurance, what is often included, what is usually excluded and how to compare policies without choosing cover that looks cheaper but leaves a gap when you need it.

blocks.heading: The main types of pet insurance

cells: Lifetime
A vet-fee limit renews each policy year while the policy remains active and premiums are paid. Ongoing eligible conditions can continue to be covered within the renewed limit.
Owners who want stronger protection for long-term or recurring illness.
Premiums can rise at renewal and you must keep renewing to preserve ongoing cover.
Maximum benefit
A fixed amount is available for each condition. Once the condition limit is used, that condition is no longer covered.
Owners who want more than accident-only cover but may not want lifetime premiums.
Long-term conditions can run out of cover.
Time-limited
A condition is covered for a fixed period, often 12 months, or until the condition limit is reached, whichever comes first.
Owners looking for lower-cost protection against short-term problems.
Ongoing conditions may stop being covered quickly.
Accident-only
Covers accidental injury, not illness, subject to terms and limits.
Owners who want basic protection against accidents.
Illness, chronic disease and many common vet costs are not covered.

blocks.heading: Billgoose Tip
blocks.text: If you mainly want protection for long-term illness, compare lifetime policies carefully. If you only compare the cheapest monthly premium, you may accidentally choose a policy where cover for an ongoing condition stops after a limit or time period is reached.

blocks.heading: What pet insurance is usually designed to cover
items: Vet fees for eligible illness or injury, up to the policy limit.
Diagnostic tests, consultations, surgery, medication and hospitalisation where covered by the policy.
Complementary treatment such as physiotherapy or hydrotherapy, if included or recommended by a vet.
Dental treatment when linked to an accident or illness, depending on the policy wording.
Third-party liability for dogs, which may help if your dog causes injury or property damage.
Advertising and reward if your pet is lost or stolen.
Death from illness or accident, subject to age limits and conditions.
Boarding kennel or cattery fees if you are hospitalised for a qualifying period.
Holiday cancellation or overseas emergency cover where the policy includes travel benefits.

blocks.heading: What is usually not covered?

cells: Pre-existing conditions
Many policies exclude illness, injury or symptoms that existed before the policy started. Some specialist policies may consider certain conditions if declared and accepted.
Policy wording, limits, waiting period and whether cover can be added or accepted by underwriting.
Routine and preventative care
Vaccinations, flea and worm treatment, grooming, claw clipping, routine check-ups and routine dental cleaning are usually not covered.
Policy wording, limits, waiting period and whether cover can be added or accepted by underwriting.
Neutering and pregnancy
Neutering, pregnancy, giving birth and treatment of offspring are usually excluded unless linked to a covered complication.
Policy wording, limits, waiting period and whether cover can be added or accepted by underwriting.
Behavioural treatment
May be excluded or limited unless referred by a vet and included in the policy.
Policy wording, limits, waiting period and whether cover can be added or accepted by underwriting.
Food and supplements
Normal food is usually excluded. Prescription diets may be limited or excluded depending on the wording.
Policy wording, limits, waiting period and whether cover can be added or accepted by underwriting.
Breed or working use restrictions
Some breeds, working animals or pets not permanently in the UK may be restricted or excluded.
Policy wording, limits, waiting period and whether cover can be added or accepted by underwriting.
Waiting periods
Illness or injury arising during the first days or weeks of a policy may not be covered.
Policy wording, limits, waiting period and whether cover can be added or accepted by underwriting.
Dental exclusions
Routine dental care is usually excluded, and illness-related dental cover may require annual check-ups.
Policy wording, limits, waiting period and whether cover can be added or accepted by underwriting.

blocks.heading: How vet-fee limits work

items.title: Check the annual or condition limit
items.description: A lifetime policy may give a yearly limit that renews. Maximum-benefit and time-limited policies may set limits by condition.

items.title: Check whether the limit renews
items.description: For long-term illness, this is crucial. A condition that needs treatment every year may need a policy where eligible cover renews annually.

items.title: Check inner limits
items.description: Some policies have sub-limits for scans, dental, complementary treatment, behavioural treatment or overseas cover.

items.title: Check the excess and co-payment
items.description: You usually pay an excess towards a claim. Older pets may also have a co-payment, meaning you pay a percentage of the remaining vet bill.

items.title: Check direct-claim options
items.description: Some vets will claim directly from the insurer, but others may require you to pay first and claim back. Ask before treatment if cash flow matters.

blocks.heading: Pre-existing conditions: the detail that catches people out
paragraphs: Pre-existing conditions are one of the most common reasons a pet insurance claim may be declined. A condition may be treated as pre-existing if symptoms, treatment, advice or investigation happened before the policy began, even if there was no formal diagnosis at the time.

This is why switching pet insurer can be more complicated than switching other types of insurance. If your pet has developed an ongoing condition under an existing policy, a new insurer may treat it as pre-existing and exclude it.
Do not hide previous symptoms or treatment. Insurers can check veterinary records when assessing a claim. If in doubt, declare the issue and ask for written confirmation of how it will be treated.

blocks.heading: Choosing the right cover for your pet

cells: New puppy or kitten
You may be able to start cover before health issues develop.
Compare lifetime cover early if long-term protection is important.
Older pet
Premiums may be higher and co-payments more common.
Compare age limits, excess, co-payment and renewal terms.
Breed with known risks
Some breeds have higher risk of specific conditions.
Check breed restrictions, vet-fee limit and condition exclusions.
Pet with previous illness
New policies may exclude related conditions.
Ask how pre-existing conditions are treated before switching.
Multi-pet household
Multiple policies can become expensive.
Check multi-pet discounts but compare cover quality separately.
Budget-focused owner
Lower premiums may mean lower cover limits or more exclusions.
Compare accident-only, time-limited and lifetime options honestly.

blocks.heading: How to compare pet insurance properly
items: Policy type: lifetime, maximum benefit, time-limited or accident-only.
Vet-fee limit and whether it renews each year.
Excess and any co-payment, especially for older pets.
Waiting periods for accident and illness claims.
Pre-existing condition wording and veterinary record checks.
Dental, complementary treatment, behavioural and prescription food limits.
Third-party liability for dogs.
Cover for lost or stolen pets, boarding fees and holiday cancellation.
Age limits, breed restrictions and whether premiums may rise at renewal.
Whether your vet can claim directly from the insurer.

blocks.heading: Self-insuring: an alternative, but not risk-free
paragraphs: Some pet owners choose to save money each month instead of buying insurance. This can work if you have enough savings to cover unexpected treatment, but vet bills can arrive suddenly and may be much higher than the amount saved.

Self-insuring also does not recreate third-party liability cover for dogs or wider benefits such as boarding fees. It may be an option for some households, but it should be a deliberate decision based on savings, risk tolerance and the pet's health, not simply a reaction to a high premium.

blocks.heading: Before You Buy
blocks.text: Ask yourself: could I afford a large emergency vet bill tomorrow? If not, a cheaper policy with meaningful cover may be safer than no cover at all.

blocks.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
items: Choosing by monthly price without checking policy type.
Assuming all policies cover long-term illness.
Switching insurer after a diagnosis without checking pre-existing condition exclusions.
Underestimating the importance of the vet-fee limit.
Ignoring excess, co-payment and inner limits.
Assuming routine care such as vaccinations and neutering is covered.
Not declaring previous symptoms, medication or investigations.
Forgetting to check dental conditions and annual check-up requirements.
Letting a policy lapse and losing cover for ongoing conditions.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare pet insurance?
blocks.text: A good pet insurance policy should fit your pet, your budget and the level of risk you are comfortable carrying. Compare more than the monthly price: look at how the policy works when a real claim happens.

hero.heading: SIM-Only vs Phone Contract: Which Offers Better Value?

image.alt: Phone and SIM card on a balance scale

blocks.text: SIM-Only vs Phone Contract: Which Offers Better Value?

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: SIM-only is often better value if you already have a phone you are happy with, can buy a handset separately, or want flexibility. A phone contract can make sense if you need a new device now, want to spread the handset cost, and the total contract cost is competitive. The fair comparison is not monthly price alone. Compare the handset cost, airtime cost, upfront fee, contract length, price rises, coverage, data allowance and what happens when the minimum term ends.

blocks.heading: What is the difference between SIM-only and a phone contract?
paragraphs: A SIM-only plan gives you the mobile service: data, calls and texts. You use it in a phone you already own, a phone you buy separately, or a refurbished device. SIM-only plans can be rolling monthly, 12-month, 18-month or 24-month deals depending on the provider.

A phone contract usually combines a handset with an airtime plan. You pay a monthly amount over a fixed term and may pay an upfront cost. Some providers split the handset finance and airtime agreement clearly; others present the package as one monthly price.
Neither option is automatically better. SIM-only usually wins on flexibility and lower monthly cost. Phone contracts usually win on convenience and spreading the cost of a new device.

blocks.heading: The value test: compare the total cost, not just the monthly payment

items.title: Find the handset price
items.description: Use the cash price of the phone you actually want, not the launch price of a different storage size or colour.

items.title: Find the SIM-only cost
items.description: Multiply the monthly SIM price by the contract length and include any activation or delivery costs.

items.title: Find the phone-contract cost
items.description: Multiply the monthly contract price by the minimum term and add any upfront handset cost.

items.title: Add future price rises
items.description: For new contracts, any automatic price rises written into the contract must be shown in pounds and pence upfront.

items.title: Value the extras realistically
items.description: Only count streaming subscriptions, roaming passes, trade-in bonuses or rewards if you would use them and meet the conditions.

items.title: Compare like with like
items.description: Use the same data allowance, network coverage and contract length wherever possible.

blocks.heading: A Quick Example
blocks.text: Imagine a phone contract costs £42 a month for 24 months with £29 upfront. The total is £1,037 before any price rises. Buying the phone for £699 and taking a £10 monthly SIM-only plan for 24 months totals £939. In that example, SIM-only is cheaper, but it needs more money upfront. Change the phone price, trade-in value or SIM price and the answer can change.

blocks.heading: When SIM-only is usually better value
items: Your current phone still works well and receives the updates you need.
You can buy a handset outright, refurbished or through a cheaper separate finance option.
You want a shorter commitment, such as a 30-day or 12-month plan.
You want to switch network easily if coverage or service is poor.
You do not need the latest flagship phone.
You want to avoid paying for a handset after the phone has effectively been paid for.
You mainly care about data allowance, network coverage and monthly cost.

blocks.heading: When a phone contract can make sense
items: You need a new phone now and do not want to pay the full handset price upfront.
The provider is offering a genuinely competitive handset-and-airtime package.
You value convenience and want one bill for the device and plan.
You are confident you will keep the phone and network for the full minimum term.
The bundle includes extras you would otherwise pay for, such as roaming or entertainment.
The total contract cost still compares well against buying the phone and SIM separately.

blocks.heading: SIM-only versus phone contract: side-by-side

cells: Monthly cost
Usually lower because it only covers airtime.
Usually higher because it includes handset and airtime.
Upfront cost
Higher if you need to buy a phone separately.
Can be lower upfront, depending on the deal.
Flexibility
Often more flexible, especially 30-day plans.
Usually tied to a longer minimum term.
Best for
People keeping a phone or buying separately.
People who want a new phone now and can commit.
Risk
Old phone may fail or lose support sooner.
You may overpay if the handset element is not good value.
Switching
Usually easier when out of minimum term.
May involve early termination charges if still in contract.
Best comparison metric
Monthly airtime plus handset ownership cost.
Total contract cost over the full minimum term.

blocks.heading: Do not forget coverage
paragraphs: A cheap SIM is not a good deal if the signal is weak where you live, work or travel. Coverage can vary by network, building, street and indoor location. Before switching, check the provider coverage map and use Ofcom's mobile coverage checker for your postcode.

Also check whether the deal uses 4G, 5G or both, whether 5G is included at no extra cost, and whether your phone supports the network bands and services you need. A 5G plan will not help if your handset is 4G-only or 5G coverage is weak where you use it most.

blocks.heading: How much data do you actually need?

cells: Light user
1-5GB
Messaging, maps, occasional browsing and Wi-Fi at home.
Everyday user
Social media, music, browsing and some video away from Wi-Fi.
Heavy user
Frequent video, hotspot use, travel or limited home Wi-Fi.
Very heavy user
Unlimited
Useful if you stream heavily, tether often or use mobile as a broadband backup.

blocks.heading: Check roaming, tethering and fair-use rules
paragraphs: Roaming can make or break a mobile deal if you travel. Some networks include EU roaming, some charge daily fees and some set fair-use limits. Check roaming destinations, data limits, daily charges and whether your usual destinations are included.

Tethering, also called hotspot use, matters if you use your phone to connect a laptop or tablet. Many plans allow tethering, but heavy hotspot use can burn through data quickly. Unlimited plans may still have fair-use or traffic management rules.

blocks.heading: What about refurbished phones?
paragraphs: A refurbished phone plus a SIM-only plan can be a strong value option. It can reduce the upfront handset cost while still giving you flexibility over your airtime plan. Check the battery health, warranty, condition grade, network lock status and whether the phone will receive software and security updates for long enough.
Refurbished does not always mean cheap enough. Compare it with the cost of a new handset, manufacturer finance and phone-contract offers before deciding.

blocks.heading: How to switch mobile provider
paragraphs: If you want to keep your number, Ofcom says you can text PAC to 65075. Your provider must reply with the switching code and important information such as early termination charges. If you want a new number, text STAC to 75075. If you only want to check whether you are still in contract, text INFO to 85075.

A switching code is valid for 30 days. Give it to the new provider when you order. Keep your old SIM active until the switch has completed and check that calls, texts, data and any banking or two-factor authentication messages work on the new SIM.

blocks.heading: Watch out for price rises and contract summaries
paragraphs: For new phone, broadband and pay-TV contracts, Ofcom rules require any price rises written into the contract from January 2025 to be shown upfront in pounds and pence, and providers must explain when those changes happen. That makes it easier to compare, but you still need to include rises in your total-cost calculation.

Providers must also give contract information and a short contract summary before you sign. Read the monthly cost, minimum term, early termination terms, data allowance, roaming, speed/coverage limitations and any separate handset finance terms.

blocks.heading: A simple decision checklist

items.title: Do you like your current phone?
items.description: If yes, SIM-only should be your first comparison.

items.title: Can you afford to buy the phone separately?
items.description: If yes, compare outright purchase plus SIM-only with the phone contract.

items.title: Is the phone contract total cost competitive?
items.description: If no, the lower upfront cost may be hiding poorer value.

items.title: Will you stay with the network for the full term?
items.description: If no, avoid long commitments or check exit charges carefully.

items.title: Does the network work where you need it?
items.description: If no, price is irrelevant.

items.title: Does the data allowance match your real usage?
items.description: If no, adjust before comparing prices.

items.title: Are roaming and hotspot rules important?
items.description: If yes, check them before ordering.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare mobile deals?
blocks.text: The best-value choice is the one that gives you the phone, data, coverage and flexibility you actually need at the lowest realistic total cost. For many people, that means keeping a phone for longer and switching to SIM-only. For others, a well-priced phone contract is a practical way to spread the cost of a device.

hero.heading: What Information Do You Need for a Car Insurance Quote?

image.alt: Documents and items needed for a car insurance quote

blocks.text: What Information Do You Need for a Car Insurance Quote?

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: To get an accurate car insurance quote, you usually need details about you, your licence, your address, the car, how the car is used, annual mileage, where it is kept overnight, named drivers, claims or accidents, convictions, no-claims discount, cover level, excess and optional extras. The more accurate the information, the more reliable the quote and the lower the risk of problems if you need to claim.

blocks.heading: Why accurate quote information matters
paragraphs: Car insurance quotes are based on risk. Insurers look at the driver, the vehicle, where it is kept, how it is used and the type of cover requested. Different insurers use different rating approaches, so the same details can produce very different prices.

It can be tempting to rush through a quote form, especially when you only want a rough price. But inaccurate answers can create problems later. A policy is built around the information you provide. If something material is wrong, an insurer may change the premium, apply restrictions, reduce a claim payment or in serious cases treat the policy as invalid.
A little preparation makes comparison faster. It also helps you compare like with like, rather than choosing a cheap quote that is cheap because it is missing the cover or details you actually need.

blocks.heading: What you need to have ready

items.title: Personal details
items.description: Name, date of birth, address, contact details, occupation and relationship status where requested.

items.title: Licence details
items.description: Licence type, how long you have held it, any restrictions and whether you hold a UK licence or another licence type.

items.title: Vehicle details
items.description: Registration number, make, model, year, fuel type, engine size, value, ownership and any modifications.

items.title: Use of the car
items.description: Social only, commuting, business use or other use. The correct class of use matters.

items.title: Mileage and parking
items.description: Estimated annual mileage, where the car is kept during the day and where it is parked overnight.

items.title: Drivers
items.description: Main driver, named drivers, their licence details, claims, convictions and relationship to the policyholder.

items.title: Claims and incidents
items.description: Accidents, thefts, windscreen claims and other incidents, even if you did not claim or were not at fault.

items.title: No-claims discount
items.description: Number of years, whether it is protected and proof from your previous insurer if required.

items.title: Cover choices
items.description: Cover level, voluntary excess, optional extras and whether you want to pay monthly or annually.

blocks.heading: 1. Your personal and contact details
paragraphs: A quote will usually ask for your name, date of birth, address, email address and phone number. Your postcode is especially important because insurers use location as one of many factors when estimating risk.

You may also be asked about occupation, industry and employment status. Answer carefully. Choose the most accurate option rather than the one that simply sounds cheapest. If your job is hard to describe, compare the available descriptions and choose the one that best reflects what you do.

If you recently moved, make sure the policy address matches where the car is actually kept. If the car is usually parked somewhere different from your home address, answer the parking questions honestly.

blocks.heading: 2. Driving licence information
paragraphs: Insurers will normally ask what type of licence you hold and how long you have held it. This can include full UK, provisional, EU, international or other licence types depending on the insurer.

If you have your driving licence number available, some insurers may use it to check or verify details. You should also be ready to provide information about any driving restrictions, medical notifications where relevant, penalty points or disqualifications if asked.

blocks.heading: 3. Vehicle details
paragraphs: The easiest way to start is with the registration number. A quote system can often identify the make, model, fuel type, year and engine size from the registration, but you should still check the details are correct.

You may also be asked for the car value, purchase date, whether you own it, whether it is leased or financed, and whether it has been modified. Modifications can include performance changes, bodywork, wheels, suspension, sound systems, wraps or changes that affect security. If in doubt, declare the change and let the insurer decide whether it matters.

blocks.heading: Vehicle detail checklist

cells: Registration number
Helps identify make, model, age and engine details.
Check the vehicle returned is the right version.
Vehicle value
Used for pricing and claim settlement context.
Use a realistic market value, not the price you wish it was worth.
Ownership
Insurer may ask whether you own, lease or finance the car.
Be accurate if the car is in a partner or parent name.
Modifications
Changes may affect theft, performance or repair risk.
Declare cosmetic and performance changes where asked.
Security
Alarms, immobilisers, trackers and garaging can affect risk.
Only claim fitted security that actually exists.
Import status
Imported cars may need specialist handling.
Check whether it is a UK model, parallel import or grey import.

blocks.heading: 4. How you use the car
paragraphs: The class of use tells the insurer what you do with the car. Social, domestic and pleasure use is different from commuting to one place of work. Business use is different again. Choosing the wrong use class can cause problems if you claim after a journey that was not covered.

Be clear about commuting, school runs, multiple workplaces, visiting clients, carrying tools or using the car for delivery work. Some uses are excluded from standard policies and may need specialist cover.

blocks.heading: 5. Annual mileage and parking
paragraphs: You will usually be asked how many miles the car will cover in a year. Use MOT history, service records, mileage since purchase or previous insurance documents as a guide. Do not choose an unrealistically low number just to reduce the premium.
Parking matters too. The quote may ask where the car is kept overnight: driveway, garage, street, car park or elsewhere. Answer based on the normal situation, not the best possible situation.
A realistic mileage estimate helps avoid issues later. If your circumstances change, such as a longer commute or more business travel, tell the insurer rather than waiting until renewal.

blocks.heading: 6. Main driver and named drivers
paragraphs: The main driver is the person who uses the car most. Named drivers are additional people allowed to drive the car under the policy. Be honest about who the main driver really is.

Putting a lower-risk person down as the main driver when someone else is the real main driver is often called fronting. It can invalidate insurance and may be treated as fraud. Adding an experienced named driver can sometimes reduce a premium, but only if the arrangement reflects real use.

blocks.heading: 7. Claims, accidents and convictions
paragraphs: Insurers commonly ask about claims, accidents, thefts, losses and motoring convictions for a set number of years. The exact period can vary by insurer and by question, so read carefully.

Do not ignore an incident because you were not at fault or because you did not claim. If the question asks about accidents or losses, the insurer may expect you to include incidents even where no claim was paid. Keep previous insurer letters, claim references and dates if you have them.

blocks.heading: 8. No-claims discount
paragraphs: Your no-claims discount, sometimes called no-claims bonus, is the discount built up for years without a claim. You will usually need to know how many years you have and may need proof from your previous insurer.

Protected no-claims discount is not the same as a guarantee that your overall premium will not rise after a claim. It generally protects the discount itself, but the underlying price can still change because the insurer may reassess risk.

blocks.heading: 9. Cover level, excess and optional extras
paragraphs: Before comparing prices, decide what level of cover you want and what excess you can afford if you need to claim. A higher voluntary excess can lower the premium, but it only makes sense if you could comfortably pay it.

blocks.heading: Cover level basics

cells: Third party only
Covers damage or injury you cause to others, but not damage to your own car.
Legal minimum for road use, but not always the cheapest option.
Third party, fire and theft
Adds fire and theft cover for your car.
Can suit some lower-value cars, but compare with comprehensive.

blocks.heading: 10. Policy start date and payment method
paragraphs: You will need a policy start date. Make sure there is no gap if your current policy is ending, because it is illegal to drive a vehicle on a road or in a public place without at least third-party insurance.
You may also choose between paying annually or monthly. Paying monthly can involve credit or finance charges, so compare the total annual cost rather than only the monthly amount.

blocks.heading: What to gather before you compare
items: Driving licence and licence history for every driver.
Vehicle registration number and realistic vehicle value.
Current insurer, renewal notice and existing policy documents.
No-claims discount proof or latest renewal schedule.
Claims or accident dates, claim types and approximate costs if known.
Motoring conviction details and dates if applicable.
Estimated annual mileage and normal parking location.
Details of modifications, security devices or tracking systems.
Preferred cover level, voluntary excess and optional extras.
Policy start date and preferred payment method.

blocks.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
items: Guessing annual mileage without checking MOT or service records.
Choosing social-only cover when you commute or travel for work.
Listing a parent or partner as the main driver when someone else uses the car most.
Forgetting previous incidents because no claim was made.
Not declaring modifications because they were fitted by a previous owner.
Choosing a voluntary excess that would be difficult to pay.
Buying the cheapest quote without checking courtesy car, windscreen, legal or breakdown cover.
Letting a policy start after the old policy ends and creating a gap in cover.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare car insurance quotes?
blocks.text: A good quote starts with good information. Once you have your licence details, vehicle details, usage, mileage, drivers, no-claims discount and cover choices ready, the comparison process should be quicker and more useful.

hero.heading: What to Do If Your Energy Deal Is Ending Soon

blocks.text: What to Do If Your Energy Deal Is Ending Soon

blocks.heading: THE QUICK ANSWER
blocks.text: Do not wait for your fixed tariff to expire before checking your options. Find the end date, annual gas and electricity use, current rates and any exit fee. Once 49 days or less remain, you can normally switch without paying an exit fee. Compare your supplier's renewal offer with other available tariffs, check the estimated annual cost and full terms, then either switch, choose a new deal with your existing supplier or deliberately move onto a variable tariff.

blocks.heading: Why the end of a fixed tariff matters
paragraphs: When a fixed energy tariff ends, the rates you agreed for that deal stop applying. If you do nothing, your supplier will usually move you onto its standard variable tariff. That may be suitable, but it should be a conscious decision rather than an accidental one.

The weeks before the end date are valuable because they give you time to compare properly. You can review your supplier's renewal offer, look at other suppliers, check whether a fixed or variable tariff suits you and avoid making a rushed choice.
There is no guarantee that switching supplier will always save money. The goal is to compare like with like and make sure the next tariff fits your usage, budget and need for flexibility.

blocks.heading: Your seven-step energy-deal ending checklist

items.title: Find your annual consumption
items.description: Look for annual electricity and gas use in kWh. Actual usage normally produces a more meaningful comparison than a generic household estimate.

items.title: Check your current tariff terms
items.description: Record the unit rates, standing charges, payment method and any exit fees for gas and electricity.

items.title: Read the renewal notice carefully
items.description: Identify the tariff your supplier is offering, what happens if you do nothing and when any new rates begin.

items.title: Compare the wider market
items.description: Compare estimated annual cost using the same consumption figures, not only the monthly direct debit.

items.title: Choose between fixed and variable
items.description: Consider rate certainty, contract length, exit fees, flexibility, meter requirements and customer service.

items.title: Confirm and keep evidence
items.description: Save the tariff summary, confirmation email and meter readings. Check the first bill after the change.

blocks.heading: The 49-day switching window
paragraphs: If your fixed tariff has 49 days or less remaining, Citizens Advice says you can switch without paying an exit fee. If 50 days or more remain, an early-exit fee might apply, so check with the supplier.

You do not need to wait until the tariff's final day. Starting during the switching window gives you time to compare and arrange the next deal. Suppliers are required to communicate with customers approaching the end of a fixed term, but you should still keep your own reminder.
Add a reminder around seven weeks before the tariff end date. Billgoose can also use a saved renewal date to prompt you when it is time to compare.

blocks.heading: What happens if you do nothing?
paragraphs: You will usually be moved onto your supplier's standard variable tariff. These tariffs typically have no fixed end date and can normally be left without an exit fee.

Standard variable tariffs in Great Britain are generally covered by Ofgem's price cap. The cap limits the unit rates and standing charges that can be applied to eligible default tariffs; it does not cap your total bill. The amount you pay still depends on how much energy you use.

Moving onto a variable tariff is not automatically a mistake. It can provide flexibility and may be competitive with available fixes. The mistake is allowing the change to happen without comparing the annual cost and terms.

blocks.heading: Should you accept your supplier's renewal offer?
paragraphs: Your current supplier may offer another fixed tariff. Staying can be convenient because there is less administration and the supplier already holds your account details. Convenience alone is not enough to show that the renewal offer is competitive.

blocks.heading: Before accepting, check
items: The estimated annual cost using your current annual consumption.
The electricity and gas unit rates.
The daily standing charges.
How long the new fixed period lasts.
Whether exit fees apply separately to each fuel.
Whether the tariff requires a smart meter or a particular payment method.
Whether a reward or discount is temporary.
How the offer compares with other suppliers and with the standard variable tariff.

blocks.heading: Fixed again or move to a variable tariff?

cells: Rates
Usually set for the fixed term.
Can rise or fall under the tariff terms.
Bill certainty
More certainty about rates, but total cost still depends on use.
Less certainty because rates may change.
Flexibility
An exit fee may apply if you leave early.
Usually no exit fee on a standard variable tariff.
Market changes
Protects against some future increases but can miss reductions.
Can benefit from reductions but is exposed to increases.
Best suited to
Customers who value rate certainty and accept the contract terms.
Customers who value flexibility and can tolerate price changes.

blocks.heading: Compare annual cost, not just monthly direct debit
paragraphs: A monthly direct debit is a payment arrangement, not the tariff price. A supplier can set or adjust the payment based on expected annual usage and the account balance.
For a fair comparison, use the same annual gas and electricity consumption for every tariff. Review the estimated annual cost, then look at unit rates, standing charges and contract conditions.

blocks.heading: A Lower Monthly Payment is Not Proof of a Cheaper Tariff
blocks.text: A direct debit can be set too low and later increased. Focus on the estimated yearly cost based on accurate kWh usage.

blocks.heading: Check whether your usage has changed
paragraphs: Do not automatically reuse an old estimate if your household has changed. Working from home, an electric vehicle, a heat pump, solar panels, more occupants or a change in heating can all affect the tariff that suits you.

If recent bills were estimated, submit an up-to-date meter reading before comparing. Smart meters can provide accurate readings when operating in smart mode, but you should still check the figures used.

blocks.heading: Special tariffs and meter types
paragraphs: Some homes need more than a standard single-rate comparison. Check carefully if you have Economy 7, another time-of-use tariff, storage heaters, an electric vehicle tariff, a heat-pump tariff, prepayment, a Radio Teleswitch Service meter or a specialist meter setup.
Confirm that the new tariff is compatible with the meter and the way you use energy. A cheaper off-peak rate may not save money if most electricity is consumed during expensive peak hours.

blocks.heading: What if you want to leave before the 49-day window?
paragraphs: Check the exit fee and compare it with the likely saving over the remaining term. It can sometimes be worth paying an exit fee if the new deal produces a larger net saving, but future costs are estimates rather than guarantees.
Calculate the possible saving, subtract all exit fees and consider how long remains on the current tariff. Check whether the fee applies separately to gas and electricity.

blocks.heading: What happens during a supplier switch?
paragraphs: The physical supply should not be interrupted. Your gas and electricity continue through the same pipes, cables and meters while the account moves to the new supplier.

Ofgem says a switch requested as soon as possible should normally complete within five working days, although you can ask for a later date. Domestic customers normally have a 14-day cooling-off period.

Take meter readings when requested and keep a dated photograph where practical. Your old supplier should send a final bill within six weeks of the switch. If the final bill shows a credit balance, the supplier should refund it within 10 working days of sending the final bill.

blocks.heading: Common mistakes when a tariff is ending
items: Waiting until after the end date before checking alternatives.
Assuming the supplier's renewal offer is automatically the best option.
Comparing direct-debit amounts rather than annual cost.
Using estimated consumption when accurate kWh figures are available.
Ignoring standing charges or exit fees.
Choosing a tariff that does not work with the meter.
Fixing for a long period without considering a possible house move.
Switching on price alone without checking service, billing and support.
Failing to keep the confirmation and final meter readings.

blocks.heading: When switching may need extra care
items: You owe your supplier money. Debt can affect switching rights depending on how long it has been outstanding and the meter type.
Your landlord pays the energy supplier. You may need the landlord to make the change.
You are supplied through a heat network. Heat-network customers cannot normally switch supplier in the same way.
Your supplier has failed. Follow Ofgem's instructions while a new supplier is appointed.
You receive supplier-specific support or have a payment arrangement. Check how a change would affect it.
You are on the Priority Services Register. Tell the new supplier about any support needs.

blocks.heading: Ready to compare before your tariff ends?
blocks.text: Have your latest bill or online account open. Enter your postcode, annual gas and electricity use, current tariff and end date. Billgoose can help you compare the estimated yearly cost and key terms before your current deal expires.
blocks.highlightText: Ask these five questions: 1. What will happen if I do nothing? 2. Can I switch without an exit fee? 3. Which option has the lowest credible annual estimate for my usage? 4. Do the contract, meter and payment terms suit me? 5. Do I value fixed rates or flexibility more? The answers should make the next step clearer.
